notes.title: Weekly Blog 43
notes.content:
Hi everyone, Stephan here with a quick insight into the Lost Legions savegame system.

[b]Open World[/b]

With Lost Legions being an open world game there is a lot of data to save.
From the player's inventory and their current location in the world, equipped weapons,
their health and stamina values, all the way to content of chests, ownership of claimed areas, progress of personal and shared quests and the already explored areas of the map.

[b]Level Streaming[/b]

Since the world is so large we are also streaming parts of the map in and out of memory. If a part of the map is unloaded we need to save everything that needs to be restored later on when that part of the map is loaded again. Those are things like dropped loot, structures the player destroyed and built and much more.

[previewyoutube=tQkc8imswms;full][/previewyoutube]
 
[b]SPUD[/b]

To make our lives a bit easier, we are using the [url=https://github.com/sinbad/SPUD]open source SPUD library by Steve Streeting[/url]

SPUD offers a generic extendable base for all kinds of things to save.  

Each level object that has data that needs to be stored gets the SPUD interface and gets an automatically assigned ID.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/24ea37b3eae12687b68d54bd2385cc95107bddf0.png[/img]

Properties that should be included in the savegame can be simply marked with a checkbox.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/29569fd5309af8f82afb29473f0cb2709c7c09f2.png[/img]

This works great for the vast majority of level objects.

[b]Multiplayer[/b]

One area where a lot of custom logic is required is the multiplayer aspect of the game.
Since players can leave and join at any time we have to restore their data not just when the level is started but whenever they connect to the server.

This is the part I am currently mostly involved in. Making sure that player inventory is restored and that personal quest lines are continued at exactly the point you left the server.

You can look forward to finally being able to save and load your game when the next playtest starts!

notes.title: Weekly Blog 42
notes.content:
Hey everyone, Bat-El here, I’m the marketing & community manager on the project.

Our big community playtest has wrapped up, and honestly, it was one of the highlights of our summer. A huge thank you to everyone who joined in,  whether you spent hours building, tried out every combat move, sent your NPCs on wild errands, or simply ran around seeing what you could (and couldn’t) break. Every single one of you helped us push the game forward.

We’ve already learned so much from this test. Some things landed exactly as we hoped, others… not so much, and a few turned out completely different than expected (in the best way). That’s the beauty of doing this together: we get to see how you play, not just how we imagined you’d play. And that feedback is gold. Our dev team already has a long list of tweaks, fixes, and new ideas sparked by what we saw.

This summer isn’t just about testing, it was also festival season. We’ve been busy showing the game to new audiences across a bunch of events, and it’s been exciting (and a little nerve-wracking) to put it in front of fresh eyes. The reactions we got were energizing and gave us perspectives we wouldn’t have had otherwise. And the good news is: we’re not done yet. There are still more great festivals lined up, and we can’t wait to share where we’ll be next.

notes.title: Weekly Blog 41
notes.content:
Bonum diem!
It's Tim, Art Lead at Tarock Interactive, and I'm back with a new dev blog entry after quite some time. Jens and Felix usually keep you up to date on the fantastic progress we're making with Lost Legions. This time, however, I'd like to give you a few insights and thoughts on the game's graphic design.

As mentioned in the last blog post, we've been working intensively on the intro level over the past few weeks. The player starts in a Roman camp in the middle of the Teutoburg Forest and has to defend themselves against attacking Germanic tribes in the rain and darkness. 
Thanks to the support of our talented level design interns, we were able to quickly block out the level – after all, it's a fairly linear passage of the game.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/b75f44e657064b863e928992c94dc781c9ea4e38.png[/img]
The big challenge was to create a dense and immersive atmosphere – and to guide the player through the level as intuitively as possible despite the darkness of the night and the chaos of battle.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/ee37fa026bc11e25a8cbee332c54692454944cc9.png[/img]
The setting: a detailed camp hastily erected by desperate Roman troops in a matter of days and nights. It serves as a starting point and place of retreat to gather equipment before heading into battle.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/435466bf727b1b6bd8740522d27eb09af9fbf51d.png[/img]
Then comes the burning forest, scarred by battle, with muddy ground, uprooted embankments, and deep trenches.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/8e8e510f0d8a5f02e4b2713ff149ab4d52cc8bdb.png[/img]
Players pass through various checkpoints, each marked by enemy barricades. After each barricade, they learn new combat techniques and control elements. At the end, a particularly dangerous section awaits in the swampiest part of the forest, characterized by dense ferns and mystical ground fog. 
There they reach the fourth and final barricade – what happens next will not be spoiled here, of course. But one thing can be revealed: After that, the game opens up into a large-scale open-world level.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/e0996152e98da220c8c7b3d5debaad7e7786487b.png[/img]
Here, the player is initially guided subtly through the level design while another series of tutorials begins. The mood is now completely different – still dark, but more cold and mysterious. Nothing remains of the hectic battle that preceded it, except for the wounds that need to be healed.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/f6a352e2ac3b50ab9421c137e16060a38396e22f.png[/img]
The view falls on a secluded valley with an abandoned hut – a quiet, almost idyllic moment. A path through a cave follows, eventually leading out into the open. In this phase, the player learns the basics of the survival and crafting mechanics of Lost Legions. The clever placement of points of interest (POIs) ensures that the player is guided through the area to discover all the important resources and treasures.

https://youtu.be/K4lBxKuWRk8
At the same time, the lore of the world gradually unfolds. Detailed environmental storytelling creates a dense atmosphere that brings the game world to life. I'm very happy with what we've created so far – and excited about how different each section feels: from the desperate battle, to the dark ritual sites of the Germanic tribes, to the almost peaceful valley.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/42af2bb48f9aa3d854fc36ffff916d229999c68d.png[/img]
We've also learned a lot in the art department – about the engine, our set dressing processes, and optimizing our workflow. Performance issues, shader problems caused by engine updates (yes, I'm looking at you, Felix), new plugins, feature changes, quests, and progression – all of these things are part of our daily world-building routine.
Earlier playtests already made it clear that our player guidance wasn't always intuitive. But with the latest adjustments to the level design and set dressing, we've been able to get this problem under control much better.

I hope you like the impressions – and I'm very excited to see how it feels to roam our world when you get to experience Lost Legions for yourselves soon.

Now we're moving full steam ahead into the next big region. Stay tuned – ad iterum!
Tim

notes.title: Weekly Blog 40
notes.content:
[p]Salvete amici mei,[/p][p]The last few weeks have been a rollercoaster of emotions for me. I’ve never been on a rollercoaster. I don’t need that kind of thrill in my free time—I already get plenty of it at work.[/p][p]Last month was supposed to be a triumphant event. I had already written about it in a previous blog. We met with the sport fencers of the Gladiatores Berolinenses in the halls of the S4G School for Games to record their authentic movements for Lost Legions. My expectations were very high. I knew that with the Rokoko Smart Suit we had good technology and that the pipeline to process and bring the recordings into the game was working. The dress rehearsal went excellently, which in theatre is considered a bad omen. The gladiators came in a group of four with great enthusiasm and loads of equipment. I was sure this would be a grand slam.[/p][p]
[/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/97e763957c0b5eedcbb939a69beaf84ab27f025d.png"][/img] [/p][p]Then everything that could go wrong did go wrong. The WiFi connection broke down. The Rokoko Studio software had trouble recognizing the suit and its components. The sensors acted up, and eventually we had a total failure because the right hand was permanently stuck in the same direction and one finger wouldn’t stop twitching. The three of us on the team tried everything to debug the problems, but time kept passing and we eventually had to abort. A big thank-you here to the team and especially the gladiators, who endured the situation with angelic patience.
[/p][p]What went wrong? The WiFi failed because someone on the team unknowingly swapped the router’s power socket with a fan. It took a while to figure that out, but that was the least of our problems.[/p][p]The connection problems with the suit were certainly a consequence of the WiFi issue. I knew the sensors in the suit were sensitive to electromagnetic fields. But it didn’t occur to me that holding a real sword or shield—because of their metallic composition—would also cause significant interference.[/p][p] [/p][p]When we changed performers, the most serious error must have occurred: the sensor in the right hand was damaged and, despite all efforts at restoration, only delivered incorrect data.[/p][p][/p][p]Time to call it off. It was terribly frustrating for everyone involved—but most of all for me. These events, by the way, happened on Friday, June 13. (No joke)[/p][p][/p][p]So far in the development and production of Lost Legions, I think we’ve done more things right than wrong. Not everything we plan works out, and when we get unlucky, it’s important to learn from it and do better next time.[/p][p][/p][p]The outcome of that day wasn’t great, but we did gain a few insights. My understanding of the Rokoko Smart Suit certainly improved. Thanks to Rokoko support, the problem with the hand sensor was solved quite easily a few days later: a plug had come loose. I had to open the little box on the back of the hand and reconnect the cable. (I try not to think too much about how the day could have been saved by using rubber weapons and plugging in a cable…) [/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/a8b913a5a1f059fad6954a51347588ca40055b96.jpg"][/img] [/p][p]What stuck with us most were the conversations with the gladiators. This club, led by their lanista Daniel, loves and lives their extraordinary sport. With great understanding of our goals and deep theoretical and practical knowledge, they had in-depth discussions with the team about martial arts and ancient Rome.[/p][p][/p][p]Since then, the suit has been in use with us almost daily. The recordings are the best and cleanest I’ve ever gotten. During performance, we remind each other every time of the gladiators’ tips and rules to get the best possible results. 
[/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/58bfdff90b1c50bcac71463e578f40ec647273a9.png"][/img][/p][p]
After this detailed experience report, here are a few quick updates on development:  [/p][p]Unreal Engine 5.6: [/p][p]Felix has done it again. Immediately after the weekend upgrade from 5.3 to 5.5—which brought us motion matching and Meta Humans in the engine—5.6 went from beta to release. Since we noticed significant FPS drops and 5.6 promised many optimizations, we decided to upgrade the engine a second time within three weeks.[/p][p][/p][p]Cleaning and optimizing: [/p][p]These upgrades, along with the ever-present memory waste and instability, led us to invest two weeks to bring the project back into shape. It wasn’t a lot of fun, but the results speak for themselves. We’re quite happy.[/p][p][/p][p]New playable demo: [/p][p]Our plan was to share a big new demo with our Discord community at the end of July. Due to recent events, we’ve pushed that target back by a few weeks. A specific announcement will follow from Bat El.
[/p][p]Smooth Moves: [/p][p]Motion Matching is awesome. The new system that blends animations with stances/poses has taken my animation work to a new level. For the first time, with Felix’s technical support in the animation blueprint, I managed to depict the typical Roman combat stance with a large scutum shield in our game. The game now recognizes states like “in combat,” “carrying shield,” “in cover,” and adjusts the player character’s posture accordingly. This results in convincing dynamics and a true legionnaire feeling.[/p][p][/p][p][dynamiclink href="https://youtu.be/_PSnZ3gaNo8"][/dynamiclink][/p][p]Furor Teutonicus: [/p][p]A major new addition to the game is the changed game opening. We’ll throw you straight into the action and let you experience the end of the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest. You start in a makeshift marching camp that can no longer withstand the assault. A desperate fight for survival in the burning forest begins. 
[/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/cce7a635581a901f6e49ad33c868a71a44e007c9.png"][/img][/p][p]This is a relatively linear set-piece that gives you a taste of some content that will later have to be painstakingly earned in the open world.[/p][p][/p][p]In my next life, I’ll learn to be brief. Until then, have fun reading and thank you for your support!  [/p][p]Jens [/p][p] [/p]

notes.title: Weekly blog 39
notes.content:
[p]Hello everyone![/p][p]
Felix here with another dev blog about Lost Legions. Today I`ll be talking about a big improvement we made in one the most glaring weak spot that we had: the locomotion system. For those of you who`ve never heard this term before: the locomotion system governs what movement animations are played depending on the direction and the velocity a character has. 
Our early system was very basic and would blend between a very limited amount of walk, run and sprint animations depending on the direction the player was moving. It looked very blocky, if you looked closely you could see the feet sliding over the floor and it was the number one cause why people thought our game didn't look as well as it actually does in our trailers.[/p][p]
This is an issue that has been haunting us for a while and while we did a lot of gradual improvements to the system, we were reaching a plateau of what we could do with just Jens as animator and me as programmer. At the end of may, after yet another disappointing interaction with a potential publisher (it`s really hard right now… maybe more on this in another blog post), I had reached the end of my patience and a reckless plan took form. 
A long weekend was coming up and I would use the four days where my teammates were away to single handedly rework the entire locomotion system – shoutout to my wife for putting up with me on this![/p][p]
The fanciest system out there at the moment comes from Unreal itself. Starting with the engine version 5.4 they had introduced a system call motion matching. The gist of the idea is that you would feed the engine hundreds of animations for all kinds of directions, speeds, direction changes, rotations and so on and some magical predictive system would pick the one frame in of those animations every frame of the game to make it look as smooth and realistic as possible. Problem was, we were using Unreal 5.3 and updating the engine mid project is usually a big no-no in development. 
I had tried an update once a few months ago to see if it would be easy: the engine had crashed and the project wouldn`t open anymore… it would not be easy.[/p][p]
There were a couple of alternatives that worked for older engine versions. All of them had similar names using variations of the words advanced, locomotion, system and component. I spent two good days playing around with those alternatives but they all had disqualifying issues: no multiplayer replication, not flexible enough for all of our weapons and armors or just not that much of an upgrade compare to what we had. I had spent half of my time and had nothing to show for… It dawned to me that I might have to do the unthinkable and upgrade our game from Unreal 5.3 to the latest version at the time: 5.5.[/p][p]
[dynamiclink href="https://youtu.be/6PeoTNG4eJ0"][/dynamiclink]

The next half day was fully spent doing just that. I won't bore you with the details but plugins had to be recompiled or exchanged, deprecated functions had to be rewritten and a couple of lost functions had to be reworked. With this done the next step was to integrate Unreals Game Animation Sample Project (or GASP) as baseline for our game. Blueprints were reparented, functions we`re overwritten, hundreds of animations were retargeted, input systems were exchanged (that was a big one) and finally I had a brand new, deceptively simple animation blueprint (how Unreal encapsulates complex animation systems) that worked with our Roman character. 
Right on time too, because my time for taking crazy risks was over with the long weekend coming to an end. The objective of having something awesome to show for taking such a risk was achieved and, even though a couple more things had broken with the upgrade that needed to be fixed over the course of the next sprint, my colleagues all access to improved processes now which improved their work as well!
I can't wait for the next playtest with the community. I`m already past seeing the improvements myself and I´m excited for our fans to see them for the first time for themselves. Will it now look and feel like a lot of other modern Unreal 3rd person games? Definitely. But it´s so much better than what we had before and locomotion is not something we aim to differentiate with.[/p][p]
I`ll leave you with one last thing: the actual face I made when Unreal released version 5.6 two days after I completed the upgrade to 5.5. [/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/c87614c61871f0b22cc8832001f89ba4b71c18ac.gif"][/img][/p][p]The new version is all about performance in large open world levels…. You don’t say? – What? I’m not checking my calendar for the next public holiday! You’re checking your calendar![/p][p]
See you next time! I’m back in the pixel mines. 😊[/p][p]
Cheers,
Felix[/p]

notes.title: Weekly blog 38
notes.content:
[p]Hey everyone![/p][p][/p][p]I got a break from the pixel mines the last few weeks and got to enjoy the narrative fumes of the plot foundry.[/p][p]When we first began working on Lost Legions, we always envisioned a strong, emotionally resonant story to accompany our survival mechanics, combat systems, and conquest features. But in the early phases of development, our focus was on building the core systems—narrative had to wait its turn.[/p][p]Now, with those foundations in place, we finally have the time and structure to give the story the attention it deserves. And we've gone back to the beginning—not just of our game, but of the characters' journey—to build a proper narrative spine: the ambush at Teutoburg.[/p][p]This moment in history doesn't just set the stage for what follows—it is the wound the entire story bleeds from. That’s where we decided the game must begin.[/p][p][/p][p][b]A New Introduction: The Battle That Broke the World[/b][/p][p]The game will now open in a moment of fire and blood: the battle of Teutoburg Forest.[/p][p]Instead of waking up behind enemy lines with no memory of what came before, players begin caught in the chaos of a devastating ambush. You and your comrades are exhausted after two days of fighting and warily resting in a makeshift camp, unaware of the trap closing around you. When the ambush hits, it hits hard: chaos, shouting, fire, and death. You are outnumbered, outmaneuvered, and abandoned.[/p][p]How will you make it out alive?[/p][p][/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/ba7cd2a3d974b3b9a5eac53c4eb992389d863bb6.png"][/img][/p][p]Super early visual of the ambush location.[/p][p][/p][p][b]Shifting Our Workflow[/b][/p][p]To make this new structure work, we had to overhaul not just how we write narrative, but how we manage it across the entire game world. At the heart of this new process is our use of [b]Nuclino[/b].[/p][p]We’ve built a custom knowledge base in Nuclino that tracks every quest, location, character, point of interest, and line of dialogue in the game. Each entry includes ownership, dependencies, and its current implementation status—whether it's in concept, first draft, scripted, voiced, or fully tested. This lets us rapidly assess what’s done, what’s blocked, and where we need to focus next.[/p][p]Nuclino also allows us to link between entries with ease—so a character's quest chain can be viewed in context with all associated POIs, scene barks, and global story beats. It has become our narrative control room.[/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/53196ebe5ef2a17130d145c92b4f196fac87a1b6.png"][/img][/p][p]And with this structure in place, we've layered in production processes that keep everything moving:[/p][list][*][p][b]Modular Scene Structure[/b]: We build each major narrative moment as a standalone asset, which we can prototype and test without requiring full voice-over or animation. Although I usually personally record what I like to call a TEMU version of the voice-over so we can judge the length… Hearing your badly recorded own voice over and over in the game is super fun and totally not cringe at all.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Playtest-Gated Rewrites[/b]: No narrative beat is considered final until it's been tested both internally and externally.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Cutscene Participation Rules[/b]: We've clearly defined how narrative moments work in co-op—when players are synced into a scene, when they can observe, and when they must participate.[/p][/*][/list][p][b]Looking Ahead[/b][/p][p]We’re continuing to refine our narrative pipelines as we move toward Beta. The new introduction will anchor everything else in the game: from player motivation, to NPC arcs, to the world itself and the many secrets it holds.[/p][p]Your story begins in the rain and fire of a forest ambush—what comes next is up to you.[/p][p]I’m going back to inhale some sweet sweet narrative fumes. Next time it’s my turn to update you I’ll finally have something visual to show. Can’t let the artists have all the glory! ^^[/p][p]Felix[/p][p]
[/p]

notes.title: Weekly blog 37
notes.content:
[b]Summer Internship [/b]

Big things are on the horizon for Lost Legions. With the summer internship season underway at the School for Games (S4G), where I also teach part-time, we’re once again bringing fresh talent into the team. These internships have become a proven win-win -the students gain valuable real-world experience, and we gain momentum in production just when we need it most.

 [img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/2ecf4a75888dc013e80cf48b5970c6a957a7fa1e.png[/img]

Right now, everything is aligning: the core systems are in place, and we’re shifting focus toward integrating all our design work into actual gameplay. It’s that exciting moment where the ideas leave the documents and start living inside the engine.

[b]Narrative Overhaul[/b]

One major milestone we’re hitting this month is a complete overhaul of the game’s narrative structure. With each sprint, our understanding of the game matures. We’ve now locked in:


[*]The overall game flow and critical path
[*]Estimated playtime for completing the main campaign
[*]A detailed narrative breakdown for every phase, including:


          [*]Key narrative beats
          [*]Major points of interest
          [*]Companion arcs and interactions


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/542bde01f057bd816eb35e5a58125fef18fdc8ad.png[/img]


Our companion NPCs in particular have evolved into fleshed-out personalities. Each comes with a fact sheet covering their background, personality, and crucially gameplay role. Many companions teach mechanics or unlock new crafting and building options. They’re not just quest-givers; each undergoes a “redemption arc” that players help resolve, making them feel like real people from a real (albeit myth-infused) world.

There’s even juicy tension between some NPCs, which I personally find very fun to write. We’re not reinventing sliced bread here but we are serving a tasty, Roman-flavored sandwich.

These materials are now getting a final pass by an award-winning professional game writer. Once finalized, we’ll derive the actual in-game dialogue and voice lines, connect everything in the quest system, and begin full narrative implementation.

[b]Cutscenes & Facial Mocap[/b]

We recently upgraded our performance capture setup to include facial animation, allowing us to record expressions and lip-sync live alongside body motion. This will add a ton of emotional nuance to our cutscenes and dialogues.


[b]Gladiators in the Mocap Studio[/b]

One of the most exciting developments is finally happening: our collaboration with GLADIATORES BEROLINENSES, a group dedicated to historical Roman gladiatorial fencing. After meeting them last year for a hands-on tryout session at their ludus (training hall), we knew we had to get them into our mocap suit.

https://youtu.be/jVUqdo6iuL8?t=18

In a few weeks, we’ll record a high-octane evening session to capture authentic combat animations for use in the game. It’s a thrilling convergence of history and tech and one of those moments where being an indie dev feels especially rewarding.

[b]UI Overhaul & Weapon Polish[/b]

Meanwhile, progress continues quietly behind the scenes. Stephan is deep in an overhaul of the user interface, implementing Tim’s cleaner designs and refactoring the spaghetti that accumulated over time. It’s not glamorous, but it’s vital and we’ll all be grateful once it’s done.

notes.title: Blog 36
notes.content:
Hello everyone,

Felix here with a slightly overdue blog post.

With the alpha milestone behind us, we’re now shifting focus to building content and scaling things up. That said, we’re always working to improve the core mechanics of the game—and with that in mind, we ran a smaller, focused playtest just one week ago.

Over the weekend, our closest community members—those on our mailing list and Discord—were invited to take part in a more compact test centered entirely around combat. We set up a new test level where players could freely equip themselves with Tier 1 and 2 gear, and quickly jump into conquest and raid scenarios. The idea was to let people fight a lot and give us targeted feedback in that area. For the first time, players could also try out multiplayer and interact using our new Helldivers 2-inspired emote system.

With a more limited scope and a smaller group, we naturally got less feedback overall—but what we did get was much more focused. That’s exactly what we were hoping for. It's always refreshing to get fresh eyes on systems we've been staring at for weeks, and a lot of the comments pointed out things we knew, deep down, weren’t quite right—but couldn’t fully articulate ourselves.

I spent last week tackling one of the most pressing issues:
Players weren’t always sure which enemy they were going to attack unless they actively locked on. We’ve got a system that auto-selects the enemy closest to your aiming center, but in a crowd, it could feel unpredictable.

So—with some high-quality programmer art (meaning: it will look much better once Jens and Tim take a pass)—I added a highlight for the current target and made sure your character always faces the enemy they’re about to strike. It’s a small change, but it made a big difference in how the combat feels. I’m really happy with it, and I hope it’ll feel much better the next time you'll get your hands on the game. (And yes, there will be a next time!)

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/1d065776e6d930682c927c319670f02ab9336199.gif[/img]

These playtests have also been a bit of an experiment for us—to see if the feedback justifies the effort—and honestly? It absolutely does. So expect more chances to test the game in the near future. Most will be small and focused like this one, but we’ll also be doing larger-scale testing as we approach release and our Steam Next Fest slot. That big public demo? We’ll definitely community-test it first.

Until then, happy Easter to those who celebrate—and as always,  back to the pixel mines. ^^

Cheers,
Felix

The savegame system and the staging of the story in particular still need some fine-tuning, but our team is focusing on these issues in every sprint.

We want to provide you with regular demos that specifically highlight new content. This will allow you to experience the progress of development without having to start from scratch again and again.

The games industry continues to be challenging: many studios are closing, projects are being discontinued and funding is more difficult than ever before. But we're not letting it get us down! We remain indie developers through and through and are looking for both traditional and creative ways of funding.

[b]Fun Fact: The Varus Battle[/b]

Did you know that Roman legionaries were unable to fight in formation at the Varus Battle due to heavy rain and muddy ground? The Germanic tribes exploited the terrain perfectly - hidden attacks from the forest, quick retreats and unpredictable attacks made it impossible for the Romans to use their usual battle tactics. An example of how crucial environmental factors can be in warfare - this is also the reason why so much useless equipment can be found as a resource in our game world. 

Thank you for reading and for your continued support! We look forward to giving you access to the new demo soon.

notes.title: Weekly Blog 28
notes.content:
Salvete amici mei,

It’s been a while since I last shared an insight into my work. I believe this will also be the last blog for this year. So, it seems fitting not only to talk about current topics but also to reflect on the past year from a personal perspective.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/56ca34b975d7aca2d289c606691120db80b39e7c.jpg[/img]

Currently, we are working on a new demo version of the game. This version will also serve as the foundation for the final release. Our last working day this year is December 20th. Then we’ll head into a well-deserved Christmas break. We’re giving ourselves a gift by putting our last bit of effort into building the new version. We’ll then play it during the holidays with patience and calm, collecting initial feedback from friends and family. Armed with these insights and well-rested, we’ll finalize the demo as our first task in the new year. Then comes the exciting moment we’ve been eagerly and reverently awaiting. We will start sharing the game with you, our community. I imagine our workflow will change significantly at that point, as we’ll have to consistently integrate your feedback into our processes. In my vision, it’s akin to a ticketing system at a QA studio. We’ll categorize reports by urgency and impact level and weave them into our production schedule accordingly. With every update (at least every two weeks), there will be patch notes where you can track the adjustments. I’m very excited about this and look forward to this new phase.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/3924a0d524151afff7bc66726e1b507bdd1e4bb6.jpg[/img]

After spending much of the summer working on characters and their equipment, my main focus has shifted back to animations. Attentive followers of our blogs and posts on other channels already know: my new favorite tool is the “SmartSuit Pro II” from Rokoko. I’ve long dreamed of an affordable indie solution for performance capturing. Years ago, I experimented with iPi Soft, where I connected 8(?) PS3 Eye Toy cameras to a PC for optical-based motion capture. The results weren’t terrible, but at that time and for our purposes, they were far from production-ready. Tim will remember this.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/2c17aa4f9a08d7bce8abae52722c98b9bda88825.jpg[/img]

In any case, the Rokoko setup (Smart Suit II + Smart Gloves) promises a suitable result for our current work. The limb motion data is transmitted in real time by many small sensors via its own WiFi to Rokoko Studio on the laptop, where a 3D avatar calibrated to my measurements replicates the movements and records them. Unreal Engine can then read these data 1:1 and play them on our Metahuman-based characters. Writing this, I must pause and marvel. The tools and technologies available to us today were reserved for large budgets and specialists a few years ago. We truly live in an era of democratized game development, with all its advantages and challenges.

The motion capture works surprisingly well. Setting it up at home is straightforward but still somewhat time-consuming. Space must be cleared, the suit carefully donned and powered with a power bank, a dedicated WiFi router must be connected, and the laptop with Rokoko Studio (for calibration of the initial pose and managing recordings) set up. It takes about 30 minutes from setup to the first recording. The same amount of time is needed to dismantle it all. Therefore, it needs to be worthwhile. I usually plan for two to three hours of capturing, which is quite intense and has left me with days-long muscle soreness from these sessions.

It pays to have a clear idea of the movements to be captured. As a base, we use animations from libraries. Only when something specific is needed or we’re dissatisfied with the quality of the pre-made sequences do we create our own animations. The longer we work on the project and the deeper we delve into the subject, the higher our standards become. I assume that animation work will accompany us for a long time. We collect these requirements in a list, which I work through piece by piece.

[previewyoutube=tTxPiyhrHC8;full][/previewyoutube]

So far, my experience has been that stationary movements come across very well, and even the articulation of finger movements is surprisingly accurate. A realization we quickly reached is that a form of acting is needed to convey the desired movements effectively. Simple, civilized motions often look too bland and unconvincing in the game. I think our camera position plays a significant role. Similar to theater, where movements need to be visible even to the back rows, our solution lies in making gestures broad and sometimes exaggerated.

Unfortunately, I often encounter problems with locomotion, such as walking and running. Foot positions are often not transmitted correctly, resulting in unnatural movements and unusable recordings.

Once I’ve captured the raw material, I can load it into the engine to connect it with our Metahuman. From there, I export the asset and load this file into Blender for further editing and cleaning up the animations. This may sound cumbersome but is quite simple and ensures maximum compatibility for me. I no longer need to retarget in Unreal.

For further editing, I’ve developed a reliable system using NLA (Non-Linear Animation Editor) actions. This allows me to select the appropriate raw material from many recorded variants and prepare it with layers for corrections and blending transitions for in-game use. Thanks to motion capture, we always have a solid foundation for our movements, and by applying traditional animation methods professionally, we can further refine and even modify the data for various use cases. It’s very exciting and educational work.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/efc133cb2a8ac98aac93bad99c807aeb66d3a799.gif[/img]

In this work, I love combining modern digital technology with physical acting. Transferring an element of reality into a computer game, comparable to photogrammetry, fascinates me. I’m thrilled that we can use such methods with our means. Sometimes, I wish I could spend my entire day doing this, but as I’ve often mentioned, in a small team, we wear many hats, and the next urgent, important, unplanned task is always waiting around the corner to surprise me.

Finally, I want to share some reflections on the past year:
Firstly, I haven’t gained any surprising new insights. If you want to follow my thoughts in detail, feel free to check out my previous blogs. It’s been an educational year, filled with many first-time experiences. We boldly embarked on the project with much uncertainty and were then overwhelmed by your positive response to the announcement of Lost Legions. Along with the industry’s strong support for our endeavor, we’ve gained the confidence over the year to make our game bigger and more beautiful than we initially envisioned. This inevitably led us to invest a lot of effort in finding suitable partners. Working with the highly talented S4G students and the resulting Gamescom demo gave us a taste of the upcoming production phase and put the functions into a playable context for the first time. This also led to an improved understanding of the DNA of our game. I enter the new year with the belief that we are ready for the next phase, and I look forward to seeing the game grow and sharing a playable version with you very soon!

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/2c9e1204a572467280249ed7bd44466a4a3ede0e.jpg[/img]

To everyone I won’t personally reach by then: Happy Holidays, IO SATURNALIA, and a Happy New Year! Stay healthy, and see you on the other side!

notes.title: Weekly Blog 27
notes.content:
Hi everyone,

It’s Felix again with a continuation of our combat redesign. We’re all very hard at work to get a demo of the game to test in a closed alpha with you as soon as possible so it might be a bit shorter than what you may be used to from me.

Like last time I’m going to use a selection of screenshots from the presentation I made to our team when the new system was invented and this time I can actually also attach a few screenshots from the game as I implemented the Tier 1 version of the system just last sprint. Let’s jump straight in:

When designing the system I wanted to solve the following issues we had with our very basic system:


[*]There was no system that rewards player choice when it comes to armor or weapons -> bigger was always better
[*]We have a limited amount of historical armor to rely on and they are not very diverse gameplay wise
[*]We have no system for injuries

In order to solve these issues I - as always - stole a bunch of ideas from some of the games whos design appealed most to me:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/9a184f630dc37e4ffa370b147b4dfd0f5353dc5c.png[/img]

The first step was to separate our health meter into a heal and an armor meter. This would enable armors to be used for what they were actually intended for, namely prevent injuries completely. With that out of the way I took a look at the health meter specifically:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/e3b39e31d3106d10b91d72288323086fd044e990.png[/img]

The idea here is that a lot of hits you get in combat, especially if you are armored, don’t result in life threatening injuries. When you do get an injury however it needs to be treated properly, which requires the proper equipment (bandages, splints, etc) and recovery, which we abstract through cooked food that the character has to ingest in order to fully heal one of the bars in the health meter. One bar emptying in combat can result in an injury that needs to be treated fast, like a bleed, and that will force the players to find a break in the battle to tend to it. I shamelessly stole this from Hunt: Showdown which always stresses me out when I start bleeding or burning in the middle of a shootout. The visual changes to the character depending on the health bars they have left are a nice feedback as well.

On to the armor next:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/e7458bfed68a9b9af53b96776e55029e7b61369d.png[/img]

Just like with health we split the armor into bars. It does not regenerate but it can be maintained up to the bar that is currently. Once a bar breaks it becomes very hard to repair. We’re currently thinking of having repair as a late game tech. This gives us the opportunity to use the limited amount of armor we have throughout the game as you’ll be able to find cutting edge armor early on that is almost completely broken. Still good but it won’t hold for long.

Here’s two in-game shots showing the difference between a pristine lorica and a pretty banged up one:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/2ee3e90bdbe1022fb92cad652b2a97929fb6112a.png[/img]


Last but not least there is the armor and damage type. This is where we give players a reason for equipping different armors and carrying various weapons:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/684bd4010106695f9a4f74889752917eddc7b6b0.png[/img]

It’s all pretty standard. Three types of armor, three types of damage and it follows a rock paper scissors system. One thing to note from this slide is that armors lose effectiveness the more damaged they are. So even if you keep bashing an armor with the wrong weapon you’ll eventually break it down and start doing damage.

As always this is in flux and when we implement and test all of it there will be changes. For now I’m happy with the theory and I’m excited to see it in action.

That’s it from me today. I’m going back to the pixel mines to work on stealth kills today. ^^

Cheers,
Felix

notes.title: Weekly Blog 25
notes.content:
Heya, it’s Uschi again! And let me tell you, my respect for ancient Rome's legionaries got so much deeper after our newest endeavor! But let me start at the beginning:

We want to make a game that is not only historically inspired but also fun to play - and one of the mechanics for that is fighting. Obviously, when you make a game where you play as someone from the roman army you HAVE to fight. And that comes with a few challenges as game developers. We have to make sure, fighting works smoothly, is fun and engaging but also kind of realistic. Now, we have meetings and discussions about combat design - maybe someone of us will make another post about it in the future. But one important factor in how fighting will feel is how it will look - what animations will happen when our players push a button. 
One of the best ways to go with animations is to capture them with motion capture (mo-cap or mocap) - but none of us are proficient with a sword or a shield. But I do have a friend who fences, and somehow thanks to a friend of a friend of a friend he recommended the guys and gals of a gladiator school in Berlin. Funnily enough - they were the same ones Bat-El and Felix encountered at the Römerfest Augusta Raurica. So Jens reached out.

And somehow on one Friday evening Jens, Tim and I found ourselves amidst the fighters of Gladiatores Berolinenses. They were so kind as to invite us to visit one of their training sessions - and to train with them! Thus began a truly truly interesting three hour course - from different techniques on how to stab with a sword, to how to move forward, use a shield not only for defending but also attacking, all with great explanations and so much information. We got to experience firsthand how much a helmet can withstand if you’re brave and face towards the fight (Tim got hit on his head so hard - and hit back so hard it put a huge dent into one helmet, but not the other person's skull). The troupe has a huge variety of different weapons and shields we all got to see (and hold - some of them are HEAVY), they even had a shield that would have been used by the german warriors and I got more info on how they would have used that shield to their advantage.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/235b462eaabf60ee4a4c424e8df26b8d2b59617d.jpg[/img]

Then we saw all of them in action as they actually fought against each other in battles! We made so many videos and photos for references, we saw so many different techniques on how to dominate in a fight, it was astonishing. They had different pairings that would have fought in ancient Rome, and we got to see how different weapons would have been used. And then it was time to experience it firsthand as we each stood our ground in our first real fight. And let me tell you, it was SO MUCH FUN!
Don’t get me wrong, it was hard, the shields are heavy and hitting an experienced guy who knew how to block was nearly impossible - but we all had our own way to at least try. And after trying to dribble, stab, feint, outmaneuver or leverage, we were pretty exhausted and truly understood how fit someone who fought for a living in that time must have been.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/9990e15bcdcecae8a274d5fe2a6d0ea3df101059.jpg[/img]

Now, we know - and they also told us multiple times, gladiators and legionaries fought differently and some of the things we saw would not have happened on the battlefield of the Teutoburg Forest. But it was soooo interesting and inspiring! I think we all will take some of the things we learned that evening and bring notes of it into our game, like how combat could work, little lore notes about equipment or even inspiration for characters. Also I think it won’t be the last time we will visit the Gladiator School - and maybe if you’re in the area or have a chance to see them at a festival you should too!

notes.title: Weekly Blog 24
notes.content:
Procedural Content Generation (PCG) in Unreal Engine 5 for Lost Legions

Hello everyone, it’s Tim here, the Environment Artist at Tarock Interactive! Creating vibrant, realistic worlds is crucial in developing Lost Legions, and Unreal Engine 5’s procedural content generation (PCG) offers the tools that make this process easier and faster. Previously, we were using Unreal’s older system due to limited experience with PCG in a real production environment. PCG allows for the efficient creation of environments like forests, mountainous landscapes, and vast meadows, which is a huge advantage, especially for small teams like ours.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/f1ab5d444591f23abd97538aecb875e3fcc289b3.jpg[/img]

PCG in Unreal Engine 5: An Overview
The new PCG framework in Unreal 5 enables developers to generate and customize large, vibrant landscapes algorithmically. The framework offers powerful features like node-based graphs and rule-based asset placement to create complex environments in just a few steps. Parameters such as density, size, and random effects can be applied to trees, bushes, rocks, and other objects. By setting rules, we can ensure objects don’t overlap or get arranged in illogical patterns.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/54eccd163c6f466bb0977cda25954ae49eb393a8.gif[/img]

Advantages for Creating Forests
For Lost Legions, creating realistic forests like the Teutoburg Forest is especially important. Here, PCG allows me to build densely populated and dynamic forests. Setting up the system is a bit tedious at first, as we have to configure the rules for generation. Later, it’s simply a matter of filling it with authentic content.
With PCG, we can specify tree species and their spacing, where ground vegetation like ferns and bushes form dense areas, and how natural barriers like rocks or small water sources are integrated. The iterative process is much faster: instead of manually adjusting every tree and bush, I can make global changes and test them instantly. This saves development time and also allows us to easily create different forest variations for different biomes. However, there are some things to consider first: Does item collection or tree cutting work without generating over 100,000 actors? How does this impact performance, and what do we need to change to create not only visually appealing but also playable worlds?
These questions have been answered over the past few weeks, and we now feel ready to unlock the full potential of PCG in Lost Legions.

Faster Iteration and Customization
Since the environments are procedurally generated, adjustments can be made anytime without requiring a complete redesign. Changes in the game’s level design can be quickly applied across the entire world by simply adjusting the relevant parameters in the PCG system. This allows us to create flexible environments with minimal manual effort, even when new gameplay ideas need to be incorporated, such as special resources in certain biomes.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/efb4c7f6443a0d08ff0b3e991c5d7f5e1d675ce3.gif[/img]

On Discord, I’ll be sharing the process of creating biomes with PCG. Feel free to join us there to stay updated!

notes.title: Weekly Blog 23
notes.content:
Hi everyone!

Felix here and I’m happy to be back with another blog about game design in Lost Legions! This time I’m going to touch on combat design, a part of the game I’ve been wanting to get my hands on since we started working on the game.

We’ve been using an out of the box solution for the combat system so far and it’s clear to everyone who plays it or that sees any of our trailers that it just doesn’t feel right.  It doesn’t feel Roman either.

But why is that? How do you make combat feel more Roman, whatever that means?

In order to answer the first question, we’ve spent a lot of time watching gameplay videos of games where melee combat feels great - or at least much better - and comparing it with what we’re doing. We’ve looked at For Honor, Elden Ring, God of War Ragnarok, New World and of course Ryse to name a few. In addition we’ve spent a lot of time watching other game designer explain their craft, such as in this great example from Game Maker’s Toolkit:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8X4fx-YncqA

The second question was much more complex. What does it take to make combat feel Roman? There’s a ton of amazing content online that shows how we think that Romans fought back then given their equipment:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jnoiTX0xZ0Y

I love how we’re able to recreate this today to a point where that’s very probably how the equipment was used. But that won’t make for fun or impactful gameplay. There is a reason why movie and game fights are completely over exaggerated. When you’re not in the actual shoes of people in a real fight to the death, it can look like a lot of boring testing followed by sudden death. So we’ll have to approach this differently. There might be something to do on the side of formation combat and I’ve been watching a lot of content in that direction as well. But how to translate that to something usable at our scale of combat (dozens instead of thousands of people) is something we’ll tackle after the second to second combat feels good.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_GKLsHwCXx0&t

So how are we going to improve how the combat feels? Through many small interlocking systems that modern games feature and that make it all feel how it should together. I’m going to share a lot of internal design documents in this blog. Keep in mind that these things are always work in progress and will evolve over time. This is a current design freeze frame for a couple of those interlocking systems: 

[b]Snap on attacks[/b]

One of the most frustrating things in Lost Legions so far is that it’s super hard to judge how far an attack will reach, which often leads to attacks missing opponents because they stop just a few centimeters from hitting them. Same with the rotation being sometimes just off enough not to hit when doing it all manually. Most games solve this problem through a more or less visible snap on system. When you attack an opponent the system will try to figure out who you want to attack and your character will turn and approach (snap to) the enemy before striking. Here’s an excerpt from the design document showing how a target is chosen:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/e8895ebf03c427988b6017e17bbb2cf3b77d2da6.png[/img]

Since the camera turns independently from the character and you’ll be able to attack enemies anywhere around you and in or outside of your range, we’re going to need a bunch of animations to make it look good, which leads us to our next topic:

[b]Animations[/b]

The quality of our animations is something that has been haunting us since the start of this project and Jens has been hard at work improving those. I’m sure he’ll go more into detail about his new snazzy Mocap Suit and the Gladiator School we’re hiring to record our animations later on. I’m more interested in the design part of it all. Here are the design slides for the animation:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/eb3c71c0a82a5f4b653ae5ae695a2ade4fca3e22.png[/img]

This one is all about picking the right animation for the first attack, depending on where the target enemy is standing. You’ll also notice heavy and shield bash attacks that will complement our combat toolbelt and give you and your opponents more options and counters to play with.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/5848a0a3ae437f04756606ee1b96a8d9a13a1298.png[/img]

While this is all about animation timing and freedom of movement for the players during those animations.
And honestly with these two things the game already looks and plays much better. But now it’s a bit too easy and there isn’t much choice of action. Which brings me to the following points:

[b]Heavy Attacks[/b]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/5349fb3b68dd34c84491311dcc2ad10e413e9d90.png[/img]

Heavy attacks are a staple of melee combat systems and a way for players and AI enemies to take full advantage of the timidity or mistakes of their opponents and also a nice to to force players to either parry or dodge attacks.

[b]Stun Damage + Parry[/b]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/552dbb2b6990737af0a30f8d6defcdc54be5884e.png[/img]

Shamelessly copied from God of War and to a lesser extent the poise system of Elden Ring (and other Soulsborne games). Will give another way of beating tough enemies and will reward the players with fancy critical or execution moves. As you can see there are also some hints of a health system rework including multiple health bars instead of just 1 for both players and enemies.

[b]Stun + Critical Hits/Executions[/b]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/ea9cf9e89b8589d6b076ef08b2f14ccc9f649b7b.png[/img]

The continuation of the stun system, leading to satisfying and visceral short cutscenes and giving the player the option to recover a bit in battle (inspired by Doom).

There is also a whole rework of the armor and health happening and shield bashes have not been completely defined yet (I’m thinking of using them as a faster but less effective way to break a block or maybe as an interrupt for heavy attacks) but that will be a story for another time. Thanks for hanging in with me for this extra large blog but it’s just a super complex topic and I wanted to give you an in depth behind the scene view.

Most of this hasn’t been implemented yet. In fact, almost all of those systems are on my todo this week. Then we’ll still have to make the AI do all of it as well. So we’re in for at least a month or two of work for the systems to be there before we can scale up the content. But with all of the designing done I’m much more confident we’ll get something enjoyable in the game than I was a month ago.

Now it’s back to pixel mines to get this all working!
Cheers,
Felix

notes.title: Weekly Blog 22
notes.content:
Hello everyone, nice to meet you!

I'm Stephan, and together with Felix, we're responsible for turning game ideas into code and bringing the world of Lost Legions to life. It's an exciting journey, and I’m thrilled to share some behind-the-scenes updates with you.

Over the past few weeks, I’ve been developing the map system, an important component that manages regions and their ownership. This system will form the backbone of much of the gameplay, providing players with opportunities to explore, conquer, and defend various territories.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/382aec49b2b58ae3512c87c80d6a68ab1791ecc4.png[/img]

In Lost Legions, the discovery, conquest, and defense of regions will play a significant role. Owning a region grants players the ability to expand their base and unlock special benefits unique to that particular area. These advantages might include access to rare resources, strategic positions, or other game-changing features that help the player along their journey.

However, owning territory comes with its own set of challenges. Player-owned regions can be vulnerable to enemy raids, so it’s vital to fortify them with enough defenses. Managing these defenses while expanding your controlled area will be key to success in the game. We’re designing this system to offer players a good mix of strategy and action, making sure that every decision carries weight.

While Felix and I have been working on the core mechanics behind this system, our teammate Tim has been busy prototyping some of the user interface (UI) elements. Some of these will for example be used to notify players when the ownership of a village changes or when they enter a new region. It is important for us that the UI stays informative yet non-intrusive, making sure players stay updated without feeling overwhelmed.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/a12c4f41c52877f2af2481d53c69393cc8698e1a.gif[/img]

In fact, I believe that a well-crafted UI, one that keeps the player informed about what’s happening in the game world without distracting from the gameplay, is often an underappreciated aspect of game design. So we’re dedicating a lot of time to refining this balance to make sure we achieve this vision.

I’m excited to continue sharing parts of our development journey with you. Stay tuned for our upcoming blog posts where we’ll dive more deeply into specific aspects of Lost Legions, including combat mechanics, resource management, and more.

Thanks for reading, and have a great day!

Stephan

notes.title: Weekly Blog 21
notes.content:
Heya, it’s Uschi again, Tarock’s writerling and this time I want to talk about my history with the ancient world. So, obviously I don’t only love to play games, I also read a lot, and I think it all actually started with Greek and Roman myths. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/6f681b4ae72fbc6577d22926a4a1f3a3afc0b662.jpg[/img]

I basically grew up with stories about gods and heroes of the ancient world, had a kid-friendly version of the Ilias and loved the Asterix&Obelix comics. At one point I was gifted two books, that sealed my love for ancient Rome:
Quintus geht nach Rom & Caius ist ein Dummkopf 
Both tell stories about boys who make it in the ancient streets of Rome, solving mysteries, experiencing life and politics. I kind of envied them for their adventures, for their resolve and their lives in this (in my eyes) big, colorful and exciting city that felt mythical and real at the same time. 
I realized that sadly, I couldn’t go back in time to visit this grand place, but I found out that there was this job called archeologist, where you could at least learn more about it. So that’s what I wanted to be when I grew up (I think the Indiana Jones movies and Tomb Raider did cement that wish). I chose a school that would teach me Latin and Ancient Greek (much to the dismay of my mother who wished I’d choose French instead), I devoured any book I could find on Rome and its history and tried not to fail any tests (I did bad in a lot of them). I had really great teachers though, who taught me about roman warfare and the great minds of the times. I can still recite the first sentence of Caesar’s De Bello Gallico, because one teacher made us remember the first paragraph by heart.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/032a9153cf58a8e472e12d837186787c16119c51.jpg[/img]

For a time I inhaled every book I could find on anything greco-roman, but in the end I didn’t become an archeologist. Still, I think being a bookworm comes in handy. While I’m not as knowledgeable on some things as our superb history consultant Lucas (you should read our Devlogs 12&13) it helps having more than a stable basis whenever I build our game’s narrative. It also pushes me to integrate a lot of small things I learned along the way. 

One example is latin. I want to incorporate not only some of the typical sayings that would have left a Roman Legionary’s mouth, but I am also thinking of latin in quests-names or items. As a narrative designer, I know some players skip any type of lore whenever they can, but there might be some people out there who will read through every item description, every letter and listen to every interaction. So I want to give them a rich experience and maybe even tell them something they didn’t know before. Of course it can’t be excessive and a short description for example probably shouldn’t be over 2 sentences, but it should work as a kind of appetizer or incentive to go and learn more by yourself.
It probably would look something like this:

Gladius
Short Sword
Quite light but sturdy, short blade made of hardened steel. Used as a stab weapon in formations rather than slashing.

Now, I (and a lot of you probably as well) know a whole lot more about the Gladius and I could have written a whole paragraph about it, could have written more about the hilt or how it was made or used and what kind of differences have been found over time. But: it’s still a game. And there won’t be a lot of space for paragraphs. So while I’m quite sad about restrictions (even if it’s our game we still have to have common sense), maybe I’ll find a way to have an NPC talk about weapons so it would be optional to hear more about them.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/fe9b2c3cf4bc4cd61eac19b79d51b9d11be40d18.jpg[/img]

And that’s it for this time.

To make this whole devlog-thing more interactive (and to maybe expand my library) I would love to know what kind of stories or books got you hooked on the Roman Empire? Please write me some book recommendations in the comments or join our discord server and share them there!

Thanks, Uschi

notes.title: Weekly Blog 20
notes.content:
[b]In this devblog, our Lead Artist Tim Ludwig answers a few questions about the building system in Lost Legions.[/b]

[b]Can you briefly introduce yourself?[/b]

[b]Tim:[/b] Gladly! My name is Tim, I am the Lead Artist at Tarock Interactive and in Lost Legions, I am mainly responsible for environment graphics, lighting, and even the user interface design. We are a small team, and many people wear multiple hats. Currently, I am working intensively on our modular building system, which allows players to create their own structures and buildings.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/6135125d7e6d85d492bb5c84611be34f02516381.jpg[/img]

[b]What is the significance of building in Lost Legions?[/b]

[b]Tim:[/b] Our game is mainly based on the mechanics of the open-world survival and crafting genre. Building structures and buildings is an essential part of the gameplay because it fulfills several key functions. When a village is taken over by the players, it can be transformed into a Roman camp through construction measures. With a good defensive structure, an enemy attack can be held off, and a well-developed field camp can accommodate more workstations and house more powerful NPC allies. Lastly, by having a solid building system, we also fulfill the fantasy of being in a believable ancient world and feeling like real Roman legionaries.

[b]What is the current state of the building system?[/b]

[b]Tim:[/b] So far, we have been satisfied with a genre-typical, but honestly, somewhat generic implementation of the building system. The basic principle is surely familiar to survival players: you build foundations to level out the unevenness of the terrain, and then you can place wall elements on top and finish them with a roof structure. We reached this stage early on, and for the pure mechanics, it was sufficient so far. Now the game has evolved, and this area can be taken to the next level. My task is to transform and expand the system so that we can create authentic-looking Roman and Germanic structures and buildings.

[b]How do you approach this?[/b]

[b]Tim:[/b] Funnily enough, this often means taking a step back. I am working with colorful blocks again to determine exactly which parts we need and how they need to fit together to replicate the models from our reference collection. Working with these blockouts allows me to try different approaches quickly and get closer to the desired result. Only when this works reliably will the placeholders be replaced with detailed elements.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/0d51ea5387cbf8c9d054ab067c9472768661919a.png[/img]

[b]How is the building system organized?[/b]

[b]Tim:[/b] The modular system is divided into themed sets. Players will be able to equip different expandable blueprints as items to access these sets. This division helps with clarity. There are several categories of structures that can be placed. There are the typical defensive structures like barriers, traps, and palisades. These can be placed freely. The core is certainly the blueprints with modular building parts to construct fortified structures that always stand on a foundation. With these, towers, platforms, and classic buildings can be created. These parts snap together magnetically based on a set of rules. Additionally, we have a category with predefined non-modular elements, such as tents and especially workbenches and workstations. Finally, there will be at least one blueprint offering elements for detailing and decorating.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/eb3b510c42d9f531acad99d78980355201a510ea.png[/img]

[b]What unique aspects have you noticed while working on the building system?[/b]

[b]Tim:[/b] Modular systems have many advantages in games, but they tend to become visually repetitive. My goal is for players to be able to build in a way that these repetitions don’t become negatively noticeable and a believable, organic overall picture can emerge. I am very confident that we will succeed. Just by expanding with beams and half-wall elements, you can break the monotony wonderfully. At the same time, the building kit must not become too granular to ensure it remains easy and quick to use. The challenge is to find a good balance so that “efficiency players” and “creative builders” can equally enjoy the game.

Another challenge is ladders! As a player, you might not give them much thought, except that they are often not so easy to use. From a developer’s perspective, ladders are not trivial, especially in a multiplayer game. We will need ladders to climb towers, platforms, and elevated walkways. Currently, we are solving this problem with a somewhat clumsy elevator method, which looks a bit odd but serves the purpose. We can continue with this approach for now, and the final iteration will come later after more critical elements are implemented.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/75b5669adcd0af301b368859e244b2acbb25b154.gif[/img]

[b]What else do you have planned for the building system in the future?[/b]

[b]Tim:[/b] The modular system allows you to build your own constructions. We can’t prevent players from creating nonsense or structures that don’t fit the historical period. That’s just part of the freedom that the genre offers. For players who care about making their camps look as historically accurate as possible, we have the idea of offering historically credible buildings according to the rules of our building sets. These buildings are pre-designed and can be placed directly. They could serve as collectible items.

Throughout the game, several technological advancements will take place. The building elements can then be visibly upgraded and will have improved properties. Enemies will not remain idle and will present players with a suitable challenge depending on their progress.

Finally, I would like to reveal an idea I am personally very fond of: peaceful building in the starting zone. In most building areas in the game, Roman marching camps are built. Sometimes larger, sometimes smaller, but essentially functional military installations that can be smashed into pieces by Germanic raiders at any time. To mitigate the frustration of losing camps and to provide a proverbial playground for “creative builders” and Roman fans, we plan a large building area that cannot be attacked, where a few special rules apply, and players can use our building system to create a farmstead with a manor.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/bbefe73771fbdb2c8cb2737715bc81ae2d92cdb4.jpg[/img]

[b]Thank you, Tim, for your insights, and thank you for your attention to our Devblog XX! As always, we are happy if you want to continue discussing the topics mentioned with us here in the comments or on our Discord channel.[/b]
