notes.title: Weekly Blog 18
notes.content:
Hi everyone!

Felix here with another episode of our weekly blog. I’m still reeling from Gamescom. Having my own booth for the first time felt completely unreal. For three days between 10am and 6pm we had visitors from potential publishers and from the press come in in 30min intervals to see the hands off demo we had prepared for Gamescom. Pitching the game so many times in front of so many people, answering their questions and seeing their reactions was a real boon. I have the feeling I know my own game so much better and have a much clearer vision now than I did before. The biggest takeaway came from talking to wonderful people from an experienced survival games publisher/developer that hammered in how important a good fighting system will be for a game based on ancient Rome. I’ll have more to say about that in a later blog.

For now I would like to present you with the following video I made shortly after gamescom. In this 26 min long video, you’ll see a full playthrough of the Gamescom demo, where we demonstrate many of the core mechanics and features we've been developing. I’ll walk you through our vision and how we've started implementing your feedback in this early version. In English.

[previewyoutube=oFJwM_SzYHg;full][/previewyoutube]

I recorded this video as an experiment. The experience at gamescom made us realize that you, our community, are the most important part of this journey and that we want to find better ways to interact with you and get your feedback. With this in mind our discord community got the first look a last week accompanied with the following questions:

[list]
[*] What gameplay elements or mechanics stood out to you the most in the demo? Why?
[*] Were there any moments or features that you found confusing or unclear? How do you think they could be improved?
[*] Which aspects of the game would you like to see expanded or developed further?
[*] What are your thoughts on the current art style and visuals? Do they match the tone and theme of the game?
[*] Did any particular visual elements or designs catch your eye? Why do you think they worked well?
[*] Do you think the long-form video would make for a good marketing beat? Should we make it public?
[/list]

We received great feedback and I followed it up with an answer that I’m sharing with you here verbatim:

—
Thanks again for all the feedback you provided. It’s terrifying and so interesting at the same time to show our baby for the first time and read your thoughts. A bit like when you put your hands on your face in a horror movie and peek between the fingers to not miss any of the action.

In the end it was really helpful and gave me confidence that we are on the right path. The most
positive feedback was consistent with what we identify as USPs ourselves and the most negative ones mostly fit with what bothers us in the game as well. On top of that there were a lot of thought-provoking ideas in there that will definitely flow in future design discussions we have.

There's 2 ways I want to answer you as a whole:

[olist]
[*] Reflect what I took as the biggest points from the feedback to you and give you a chance to check me if I forgot something. [u]I’ll occasionally add my thoughts directly in underlined text.[/u]
[*] Answer some questions and give insights to some of the thought processes behind our decisions. Feel free to give constructive criticism there as well.
[/olist]

Here are the biggest points and questions from the feedback, I used AI to help me categorize:

[b]General Positive Feedback:[/b]
[list]
[*] Blueprint Building Mechanic: Highlighted for ease of use and thoughtful.
[*] Centralized Inventory (Global Inventory): Praised as a significant quality-of-life improvement, avoiding excessive running back and forth.
[*] Task Delegation/Worker Assignment: Smooth implementation appreciated, with potential concerns for future scaling or expansion.
[/list]

[u]This was all really cool to see as that is exactly what we wanted to shine a light on with the demo. (USPs)[/u]

[b]General Concerns:[/b]
[list]
[*] NPC Behavior/Animations: Multiple respondents found NPC animations out of sync or unnatural. [u]– This has been a pain since the very beginning. As a small team we need to develop a sturdy yet lightweight pipeline to be able to deliver facial expressions, in sync with voice over, in sync with body animations. From a technical POV these are separate channels that need to play nice with each other. We are getting there and made tremendous progress however what you see in the demo is a fast and rough treatment and basically a proof of concept. More to come.[/u]
[*] Combat Mechanics: A lack of dynamic combat stances, with requests for features like shield walls and troop formations. [u]– This is something that has been making us very excited since we had the same feedback at Gamescom. Very high on the to-do if we get an investment. We might get to improve the 1v1 combat quite a bit without any investment thanks to better animations but formations (what really excites me) will not be feasible without more budget.[/u]
[*] Character Creation/Progression: Requests for more customization in multiplayer and clarity on character strengths/weaknesses. [u]– Character customization is a bottomless pit in terms of production investment. We’re thinking of taking the path of games like Grounded where characters have predefined looks and personalities but are the same in terms of initial abilities.[/u]
[/list]

[b]General Questions:[/b]
[list]
[*] Players were unsure about the mechanics for accessing and using the command table to assign tasks. [u]– This part of the controls and the UI is still very rough. The way I ordered NPCswas by pressing Q on objects that could be assigned tasks. We will improve on this for the next public version.[/u]
[*] Some respondents felt unclear about how the stockpile is organized and whether there is a limit on storage capacity. [u]– The idea is that the stockpile is an endless storage. Potentially it will be restricted and you will be able to build boxes that will extend the capacity of the storage in general. This needs to be tested.[/u]
[*] There was a question about whether workers would stop tasks to defend the camp if an attack occurred while they were working. – The way they work now they would be slaughtered like sheep. ^^ The idea is that they switch to combat mode themselves and go defend the base and themselves.
[/list]

[b]2. Visuals & Art Style[/b]
[b]Common Positive Feedback:[/b]
[list]
[*] Armor & Buildings: Roman-themed visuals were well received, with armor and environmental textures often standing out.
[*] Hostile Environment: The inclusion of worn-down NPCs with scratches and environmental elements like burning forests added to the atmosphere. [u]- I’m sure our Lead Artist Tim will be happy to hear that. :)[/u]
[/list]

[b]Common Concerns:[/b]
[list]
[*] Art Style Uniqueness: While some players liked the gritty and realistic style, others suggested the need for a more unique or identifiable aesthetic to stand out. [u]- I feel that might be a common problem with realistic games. I’d be happy to hear more concrete ideas on how to make it more unique if you have any.[/u]
[/list]

[b]Questions:[/b]
[list]
[*] Some players were confused about how players will be notified if resources are unavailable (e.g., wood for building) [u]– Probably through a notification when the problem arises and through a visible issue marker in the management interface.[/u]
[/list]
[b]Suggestions for Improvement:[/b]
[list]
[*] Lighting & Ambiance: Some respondents mentioned weather effects, fog, and environmental animations (like tree sway) could add more depth and immersion.
[/list]
[b]
3. Narrative/Storytelling[/b]
[b]Common Positive Feedback:[/b]
[list]
[*] Setting & Lore: The Roman-Germanic historical setting was well received as unique and underexplored in games.
[*] Tone-Setting Scenes: One respondent suggested adding narrative cutscenes to set the tone of the story and help the player connect with the protagonist. [u]– The concrete idea there was to do something similar as Guild Wars 2 but with vignettes instead of an actual cutscene. Medieval Dynasties and Enshrouded do this as well. - I love it. The key I feel here is to make it as long as it needs to be and as short as possible.[/u]
[/list]

[b]Common Concerns:[/b]
[list]
[*] Historical Accuracy: Some respondents noted issues with the historical accuracy of names and roles (e.g., women in command roles) within a Roman legion. [u]– I hear you on the names thing. Definitely something we didn’t look at with our historical advisor while making the demo.[/u]
[/list]

[u]On the topic of women in the Roman Legion: We’ve heard this one a lot lately and we took some time to think about it. On the one hand of course, we want the game to be as historically accurate as possible and on the other we don’t want to exclude half of our players by being strict on this issue. The solution we came up with is the following: NPCs will follow historical findings (no female legionaries, but holding other roles and positions on both sides). The players on the other hand will be free to play whoever they want, including the most badass female Optio the world has never seen.[/u]

[b]4. User Interface (UI)[/b]
[b]Common Concerns:[/b]
[list]
[*] Crafting Indicators: Several respondents felt the UI for quick slots and crafting timers was too modest or overlapped with other text.
[*] NPC Assignment Clarity: Some confusion on how NPCs are activated to perform tasks. 
[/list]

[u]The UI is still very much work in progress. We’ll definitely put a focus on the points that stood out to you the most.[/u]

[b]5. Marketing & Publicity[/b]
[b]Common Consensus:[/b]
[list]
[*] Marketing Strategy: Respondents felt the current demo video was too long and not polished enough for public marketing. Shorter, more focused videos (e.g., clips on TikTok) were suggested.
[/list]
                                                                                
[u]I hear you. Thanks for the reality check. I’m sure Bat-El feels validated. ^^ We’ll make shorter, more specific videos about each topic. This long form video will be shown in a blog post on steam at some point to get the wider community up to speed with you.[/u]

[b]Miscellaneous/Other Feedback[/b]
[list]
[*] More Pets & Dynamic NPC Behavior: Requests for more interactive NPCs (like cooks working). – [u]We’re actively working on that. It’s a bit tricky because they will need to interact with dynamically placed objects.[/u]
[*] More animals to pet. [u]– Yes! Always! More! My secret wish is to take the doggo in battle… but then he could get hurt… which I probably couldn’t stomach.[/u]
[*] Motion Sickness: Rapid camera movement caused discomfort for one player. [u]– Super important Topic. I have no clue about that topic from a design standpoint but we’ll dive into this. We have our own motion sickness patient with Uschi that we can test our solutions on. *mad scientist laughter*[/u]
[/list]
—

And that’s it! While we’ve already gotten a lot of quality feedback please don’t hesitate to reach out with more. Join our discord server if you haven’t already to get access to more sneak peeks of that nature before anybody else. Since we use discord to work we’re also more responsive there.

Puh. That was a long one. ^^ I’ll leave you here to get back to the pixel mines. That game is not going to make itself!

See you next time!
Felix

notes.title: Roman survival game Lost Legions wants to ignite your love of history
notes.content:
When you think of the Roman Empire, its great triumphs probably spring to mind first. Its grand conquest and expansion, its political systems, and its deep-rooted influence on everything from language and art to religion and architecture. New survival game Lost Legions bears a love for the period, yet it focuses on one of the more dramatic defeats borne by the Romans - the Battle of Teutoburg Forest, where an alliance of Germanic tribes ambushed three Roman legions, leaving them scattered, and marking an abrupt end to Emperor Augustus's plans to expand into the region. I took a look at Gamescom 2024, and I'm already a big fan of the setup.

notes.title: Weekly Blog 17
notes.content:
Salvete amici mei,

Gamescom is now a while back, and the dust has settled a bit. We had a phenomenal time at the convention. During the three trade visitor days, we presented Lost Legions to the press, publishers, investors, and interesting service providers from morning until night. Our calendar was packed, so our small 2.5m x 2.5m booth was buzzing like a beehive. Every half hour, a new guest would drop by. As you know from Blog 16, the three of us were on-site and could even handle two appointments simultaneously most of the time. It worked out really well, we gave it our all, but by the week after, we were completely drained. At least, I was. It gave me time to reflect on how grateful I am that everything went so well and how much luck and support from all sides are needed to make it work. Below, I will outline the areas that have occupied us the most in recent weeks:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/274e5e415cf4772423fe53d81f35347bc09353b5.jpg[/img]

[b]Appointments[/b] You can't really get appointments at the convention itself. You should schedule your meetings in advance, weeks ahead. As newcomers, that wasn't easy, so we had help from our PR and communications agent from the U.S., our bizdev consultant, and Bat El, who reached out to all the publishers and investors we had been in contact with since the announcement at the end of April to fill the last gaps. Fortunately, most were very interested in getting an update and discussing possible collaboration with us. But imagine the stress we felt as GC approached and our calendar was still slowly filling up. All that effort, and then no one shows up? Of course, we acted totally cool and collected, not letting anything show. In the end, it worked out.

[b]Audio[/b] We don't have anyone on the team who professionally deals with audio in games. Stephan, being an audiophile, might be the closest fit. He once set up a small studio in his parents' basement. The truth is, everyone agrees that sound is super important in games, but it often gets treated like a stepchild: it's important, but somehow other things always seem more important. We are in the enviable position of having Daniel Pharos and the Audio Creatures from Berlin on board for the audio of Lost Legions. These guys love their work and make us look good, even when we’re being neglectful step-parents. Thanks to a final push just before departure, a significant batch of audio made it into the convention demo. I'm always impressed by how much good sound enhances a game and makes things happen in your mind that aren't even on the screen. Every time I experience this, I vow to treat the audio better in the future. This time, I really mean it.

[b]Historical Consulting[/b] This important topic was already covered in more detail in Blog 12 and 13 in the form of an interview. I just want to emphasize again how happy I am with our collaboration with Lukas. For me, this is a successful test run that shows how we want to continue working in the future.

[b]S4G Co-Working Space[/b] It's no secret that we're working based on grants and our own investment. We’re putting every cent into development and saving on expenses for a representative office in the city center. Anyone who thinks I don’t have a clear idea of what it would look like once we’re successful doesn’t know me well. But for now, we're trying to keep a low profile. It was all the more brilliant that we could rent a room at School 4 Games (S4G) for a few months this summer. Finally, I could escape the home office and commute to work like a normal NPC using public transportation. This opportunity is certainly thanks to the unique circumstance that I've been teaching at the school for 12 years and have known the school management since 2004. Based on this trust, we took this test and found it to be mutually beneficial. On the one hand, we have an affordable office in the city with access to the student body for game testing. On the other hand, the school hosts a startup game studio in its halls, where students can get a glimpse and our experienced developers can also offer advice and support to the students on their projects.

[b]S4G Interns[/b] As part of their training, students must complete a mandatory internship with a company. We took on 8(!) handpicked interns from the current graduating class for 10 weeks. This was the real trigger for the co-working space scenario. I want to give a heartfelt thank you to our extremely talented interns. Before their involvement, the game was metaphorically standing on an empty field, surrounded by forest with disconnected technical test areas. On the way to the Gamescom demo, and thus to the Alpha milestone, everyone fully contributed, and, in my eyes, a brilliant demo emerged, showcasing many of our good intentions for the full game. It pushed us far ahead in implementing features, developing technology, and refining our workflows. The high development speed we had this summer, thanks to the support of the students, gave us a glimpse into the future. We could experiment with what it would be like when the team grows. I can tell you, I want to restore that state as soon as possible. It brought me a lot of joy.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/d42db8683f0f4f48cf12f8d30356c32ea8704047.jpg[/img]

[b]Print Materials[/b] We wanted to leave a lasting impression on our conversation partners. Show that we mean business and that Lost Legions should be perceived as a real brand. What do the big guys do? Decorate their booth and hand out bags! For the interns, I also wanted to have a gift set ready as a small token of appreciation. So, we had to come up with ideas, create graphics and designs, and find online suppliers who could deliver the right quality, price, and timing. A big effort in terms of time, money, and nerves. In the end, almost everything worked out, and we are very satisfied with the impact we were able to achieve. Personally, I am super proud of the idea with the Roman and Germanic shields on the bag. Depending on which side you turn outwards, you show your allegiance. But don't start a fight in the convention hall if you run into someone from the other side!

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/21ed81096cee9e43648d7fb1e9d2bfee5e003d21.jpg[/img]

[b]Team Shirts[/b] Our developer shirts are their own anecdote. My wife designed them for us with the help of a Cricut plotter and appropriate foil. It was a laborious task to stick nine polo shirts on the front and back. This often happened during the night shift, amidst our work and family life, when we weren’t busy painting 50 3D-printed USB Gladii.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/36f019eaae1063bc822479f16f1a05579f4582e6.jpg[/img]

[b]USB Gladii[/b] Three weeks before the convention, it was still a funny idea: "What if we put the press kit on a USB stick shaped like a Gladius?" The hope was that everyone who received such a gem would be so enchanted by it that they would show it to their friends and colleagues, and in the process, talk about our game. Again, we wanted to show that we mean business. The 3D intern loved the idea and immediately started working on the model. I got 50 super small USB sticks. In my dad's hobby basement, the resin printer (Elegoo Mars) was running. Printing 5 sticks per round took 8 hours each(!). Everything was going smoothly until the touch display on the printer stopped responding. There were only 8 days left until Gamescom! The 3D intern managed to borrow the neighbor's 3D printer, and I also invested in a new one. After initial difficulties, we were able to continue printing. By the Thursday before Gamescom, all the parts were printed. On Friday, all the interns helped apply the base colors. It took the entire weekend, working until 3:00 AM each night, to finalize the Gladii. It was worth it, in my opinion. I love it when a plan comes together.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/ae5f952899fdd8d20403c11bbc5719dffadc6b9d.jpg[/img]

[b]Renting a PC[/b] At the convention, we wanted to showcase our game. Unreal Engine 5: Many assets and packages were quickly integrated. We also spent some time on optimization, but let's be honest… We needed a proper presentation PC with decent power. Felix might have been able to bring a suitable machine from CERN. But our biz dev agent activated the guys from Caseking, who offered a 100% worry-free package at a reasonable price for the convention setup. We jumped at the offer, after all, we're saving on office costs and I didn't want to transport our own PC via DHL or Deutsche Bahn. Bat El and Felix handled the communication with Caseking. notes.title: Weekly Blog 14
notes.content:
Hi everyone!

Felix here with another episode of our weekly blog. With gamescom only two weeks away we are all working like crazy to make the best out of our demo. I am already pretty excited by the results and I’m sure it will get even better by the time we finally get to show it off behind closed doors. We´re also working on a new gameplay trailer which showcases the latest visuals and features in the game and we´ll upload this one for all to see as part of a showcase that we´ve been invited in to participate in. The excitement - and stress level - have reached new heights. ^^

But my receding hairline is not what I came here to talk about today. Instead, let me talk about how the conquest system works that we´re currently in the process of implementing:

The world of Lost Legions is divided into areas of controls that are centered around villages and fortifications. Each of these regions provides at least one strategic advantage that makes it an attractive target of conquest. It could be rare resources like a mine containing precious ores, a strategic chokepoint like a bridge across an impassable river or a unique building like a mill. Additionally, the forts and villages will be the only places where most of the game's buildings, workstations and objects can be placed by the players.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/74b1883011647be7d21e063ccf14facc1dfbedb7.png[/img]

At the start of the game, all regions in the world are controlled by Germanic Tribes, with the exception of a very limited starting base in the hands of the Romans. The players will have to conquer enemy bases one by one in order to unlock their advantages for themselves and will then have to hold on to those bases when Germanic Raid parties attempt to conquer them back.

Starting a conquest attempt is easy: the players encroach on the area of a village or a fort and initiate combat with one of its defenders. This will start a conquest battle where players will have to defeat waves of defenders, culminating in a battle against the chieftain or commander of the location. If at any point before the village has successfully been conquered the players all leave the area for any reason - they flee, are defeated or a combination of both - the conquest will fail and the village will be reset to its original state. If the players succeed, the location will be razed of most germanic buildings and players will be able to build their own base on top of the remains. The first time players conquer a new region, they can expect to find some nice loot in the stockpile of their newly conquered camp.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/85f920b7f93c3620307f237bcede04ab1041c77b.png[/img]

The tribes will not sit idly upon being kicked out of their homes however and will mount counterattacks. As long as the players control at least one germanic location a raid countdown will tick down in the background. Once it has elapsed a raid will be launched on one of the areas belonging to players that borders on germanic territory. This means you can create safe zones by strategically conquering buffer areas around places that are important to you.
Once a raid has been launched, players will have a grace period to travel back to the endangered camp in order to defend it. The raid will involve waves of tribesmen that will try to destroy as much of the camp as possible, capture any NPCs they can get their hands on and defeat all the defending players. The raids will be more and more challenging, the more camps players control. Defeated raids will drop nice loot for the players to use. If the raiders manage to defeat all the players however, the camp will be lost and will revert to what it was under germanic control. Any items and resources left in the stockpile will remain there until the players conquer the site again.

This all sounds great in my head and we will have to see during internal and external playtests if it's actually fun. All in all I think this will be one of the major gameplay elements of the game that will drive many of the others around it.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/e8d1ef2e762d21af6d55f6c64c75f4b29f286635.png[/img]

Bonus screenshot: You can now pretend to be Russel Crow in the game. ^^

I´m looking forward to hearing any feedback from you at this level. My next scheduled blog is during gamescom, I hope I will find time to write something in between the excitement! 🙂

Until then: back to the pixel mines!

Felix

notes.title: Weekly Blog 13
notes.content:
[b]Salvete amici mei[/b] 

[b]Welcome back to the second part of the interview with our historical consultant, Lukas Grüning. As last time, Lukas discusses some personal experiences and gives deeper insights into his work at Tarock and on Lost Legions. Enjoy:[/b]

[b]How did you get involved in the development of "Lost Legions"? What fascinated you about this project?[/b]

I was a participant in a very interesting seminar at Humboldt University during my first semester, with the topic: “Cooperation between Research and Industry using Entertainment Software (Games) as an Example.” That was my first contact with Jens, who gave a lecture on the subject. In the following semester, I had the opportunity to take over the seminar leadership. I then spent two semesters managing the collaboration between the Winckelmann Institute on the research side and Jens on the business side. That was a very formative and enlightening time.

Outside of this academic level, I stayed in contact with Jens and kept up-to-date with business and project development. As a gamer, this naturally intrigued me in connection with my field of expertise. I wanted to satisfy my curiosity about how a game studio operates and how a game is created. On the other hand, I hoped to contribute, especially because one of the company's goals is to create historically grounded content, which implies a need for historical expertise.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/84f76005e0d9cdc9c01f93b948137548b175ad70.jpg[/img]
[i]Jens presents Tarock Interactive's vision to students of Classical Archaeology at the Winckelmann Institute (Humboldt University, Berlin)[/i]

[b]How do you ensure historical accuracy in the game? Can you explain how you review and advise on game content?[/b]

There are two ways of communication. On one hand, I review the already developed material, walk through the studio, and watch the 3D artist while they create the Lorica Hamata armor. I ask my colleagues how the design of the NPCs is going and simultaneously think about how I could contribute meaningfully. I don’t limit myself to just the basics, like “Yes, I see, the building part doesn’t fit,” but go into detail to preempt any future questions. For example, when researching clothing or weapons, I create a complete documentation, which also serves as a reference for my future work.

On the other hand, there are also questions directed at me. These can be quite detailed and arise from problems related to graphics or quest design. I can answer many questions quickly, while others require more time. I find the new perspectives that these questions open up from the developers’ viewpoint particularly fascinating.

It’s also interesting to see how laypeople, who often ask seemingly simple but archaeologically complex and controversial questions, such as “What color was this or that?” which, based on research, often doesn’t have a solid answer, and various interpretations must be used to maintain credibility. I communicate this complexity as well.

This brings me to another important point of my work: finding compromises. To stick with the armor example, I ask, “Why is the Lorica Hamata so short?” If the answer is that they didn’t know better, that’s an easy fix and should be adjusted. However, if there’s a technical reason, I question whether there might still be a way to maintain historical accuracy. Some deviations in detail must also be acceptable if they are marginal, barely noticeable, or not absolutely certain. After all, it’s about developing an entertainment product, so understanding the team’s working methods is also required.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/af99a7824206dabd8bc0af9b590c20095242dd46.gif[/img]
[i]The chainmail Lorica Hamata in female and male variants. The armor is adapted to the anatomy in each case[/i]

[b]What are some of the biggest challenges you face when balancing historical accuracy with gameplay and narrative elements?[/b]

I had expected to encounter more resistance. I thought there would be more criticism when I presented pedantic details. I’m happy that so far I haven’t had problems communicating content and changes. This is because everyone here is so open and appreciative. I feel that the team is really enthusiastic about this historically accurate approach.

One anecdote, however. Romans dug trenches. Period. That was the most important thing for a camp before any palisade was set up. I was told that the game’s technology doesn’t allow for terrain deformation. This feature is not planned. My heart bled a little there. I am still pushing to find a solution with the team.

Another situation arises when I am told that women should appear as soldiers in the game. I clearly communicated that this is historically inaccurate, but it can be interpreted in the context of today. Also, as mentioned, it is a computer game, and due to the unique survival situation of the characters, we have ways to convey it somewhat credibly. So, I can still sleep well at night.

In my role, I am more concerned with certain nuances that might be overlooked in other productions where I think: “Here we could show some courage.”

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/2f4b98629439b58f6ea19d47e6b88e0edeba51d6.jpg[/img]
[i]Two concepts of our playable female characters (Dorcas and Alecto) with rough implementation as Metahuman. Next step: skin and hairstyle details. All characters have a unique backstory with their own quests[/i]

[b]How do you integrate folklore and mythology into a historically grounded game world?[/b]

I have concluded that it is not anachronistic to connect mythology with actual life. This is a very ancient concept. Although we know that reality was different, many people at that time believed in it.

From the perspective of an ancient observer, one lived in a world where a mythological world existed parallel or simultaneously. This does not mean that all Romans, especially the educated ones, believed Minerva might appear to them. However, there were deeply religious people, similar to today, for whom the supernatural was part of daily life. In general, religion was an integral aspect of the state and public life. You sacrificed before a wedding or before a journey—it was just part of it. It was less abstract than the modern distinction between historical reality and mythological components. How these supernatural components are actually embedded in the narrative is another question. Essentially, I find it fits well and offers exciting added value for gameplay.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/13c2f1ded32a4c62ae87efa15e79ad9903963c08.gif[/img]
[i]In our title image, we have already hinted at the integration of Roman and Germanic mythology[/i]

[b]What aspects of game development are you most excited about, and what do you hope players will take away from their experience with "Lost Legions"?[/b]

I love immersing myself in the ancient world and viewing it through the eyes of one of its inhabitants. If I can also help shape this world, I’m happy. Lost Legions promises to offer me exactly that, and what I particularly enjoy are the details. The game world is filled with authentic elements that I can examine up close and that interact with each other. It’s especially exciting that there will be artifacts brought to life from the world of the Germans and Romans.

I am also looking forward to following the further development process. I don’t yet know everything about the game myself and am excited to be part of the creation process and to contribute to it.

As a player, I am definitely driven by story and find the concept behind the world of Lost Legions very exciting. I imagine the game will give an impression of Roman culture on the edge of the empire. That alone is a fascinating field of research. I’m most excited about this situation embedded in the historical and mythological narrative.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/c69cd23f701adc310dc027e2e3bdf1dc855d6127.jpg[/img]
[i]Lukas at an excavation in Tell Burak, Lebanon, July 2022[/i]

[b]Thank you for the interview, Lukas. You have already gathered a true treasure trove of historical and archaeological content for us. Lost Legions will be a better game because we can work with these results! I look forward to our continued collaboration and the further development of our game! Best regards, Jens[/b]

notes.title: Weekly Blog 12
notes.content:
Salvete amici mei,
Bringing this blog to a close took a bit longer. However, something special has come out of it. I had this idea for a long time and finally got around to implementing it. I interviewed our historical consultant, Lukas Grüning, and asked him about his work with us. Some interesting anecdotes emerged, which I am happy to share with you here. To avoid straining our usual format, the interview is divided into two parts. The second part will be available next week. I hope you find this new insight as exciting as I do. Enjoy with Lukas:

[b]Can you tell us something about your background and your current studies? What inspired you to specialize in the history of ancient Rome?[/b]

Even as a child, I devoured factual and audiobooks about the ancient and feudal world. I was particularly fascinated by the illustrations. It wasn't always clear that I would become an archaeologist, but after high school and experiences abroad, I knew: My interest in ancient cultures, the tactile experience of ancient objects, and the visual aspect of this lost world captivated me. That's why museums have always drawn me in. An anecdote from my Interrail days: I spent almost six hours alone in the British Museum in London while my buddy had long returned to the hostel. The next day we were leaving, but I went back for another three hours and had to literally run(!) to catch our train at the station.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/e4463287963a2f027f80338a21ba7740d53c58b4.jpg[/img]

Currently, I am a Master's student at the Humboldt University of Berlin in Classical Archaeology at the Winckelmann Institute and will complete my studies next year. I did my Bachelor's in Heidelberg, where I ultimately decided on Classical Archaeology. Roman culture is similar to ours in many ways, especially in terms of values and law. At the same time, there are significant differences, such as slavery and militarism. This mix of familiar and foreign fascinates me and drives my interest.

[i]"Philologist Uvo Hölscher already postulated in 1965 that the Roman and Greek antiquity is our 'closest foreign': The ancient world is sufficiently foreign to question our habits of thought and at the same time close enough to be relevant."[/i]

[b]What are the career prospects for a trained archaeologist?[/b]

There are indeed historical consulting firms. Conventionally, a request is made to a research institute to look at the material for a few hours. You then do the necessary work. Or you have an in-house team or person, but these positions are rare. Both in the private sector and in academia and education, there are only a few jobs for trained archaeologists. Therefore, many aim for the highest possible degree, as competition for these positions remains tough even with declining student numbers. It is therefore advisable to have a second career path. Besides working in research at universities or museums, it is advantageous to find a position in the private sector, for example as a consultant. My interest and the opportunity to gain practical experience during my education are particularly valuable in this context.
[b]
Are there specific historical sources or references that you find particularly valuable for your work on "Lost Legions"?[/b]

I use various online search engines, not Google or the like, but from libraries, scientific journals, or sites that upload the latest publications in any form of ancient studies. Sometimes I find something in digital form and have access to it through Humboldt University, but in about 85% of the cases, I have to go to the library for research. Sometimes the book cannot be borrowed, and I have to work on it on site. For this project alone, I currently have an additional 10-12 books here, with a tendency to increase.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/401988fe8ad54d8707c85f3a6e7c47659d74ffd6.jpg[/img]

[b]Can you share an example of a historical detail or event that was particularly interesting or surprising to you and how it is integrated into the game?[/b]

There was an incident that shows exactly how our joint work operates on different levels and can be applied further down the line. It involves the topic of armor. Previously, a specific variant of the plated armor Lorica Segmentata (Corbridge) was included in Lost Legions. I knew this type as the usual equipment of the legion from that time. So I wasn't surprised to see it in the game. Then, a very attentive online community pointed out that this armor was not accurate. The team alone couldn't follow up on this detailed criticism but forwarded the issue to me. Following the clues, I was able to verify that there is a specific type (Kalkriese) that is explicitly associated with the battle of 9 A.D. Notable are the pointed shoulder plates and the reduced number of ornaments. So if we know that this armor was there and the Corbridge type only appears a few years later, then we are well advised to adjust the representation to the new findings. Incidentally, my research has shown that the use of Segmentata (plate) and Hamata (chain) could have been about 40:60. So NPCs in the game will also appear accordingly equipped. That's how it works in archaeology; you do it typologically. I think this example shows a good engagement with the topic. The team presents something, it is challenged by the community, then it is reviewed, and the result is implemented in the game.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/a07172dbbb6bf119758b9fc68541fdc3ff0c711d.jpg[/img]

[b]
What common misconception about antiquity do you hope to address or correct through this game?[/b]
Hmm, what comes to mind right away, because it was just a topic within the team: You can't say that the Germans were dirty barbarians living in filth. We know a lot more about the Romans because there is much more information about them. There are many (hobby) experts who are very knowledgeable about Roman legionnaires and their armor. Knowledge about the Germans is often less. However, the Germans were very well-groomed and had various hygiene items. They invented soap and used combs, tweezers, and razors. Even Tacitus, who also portrayed the Germans as barbarians, reports that they bathed frequently and washed their hair. Not everything was dirty and pigs were not wallowing everywhere. Of course, you can't compare the living standard of a Germanic person to that of a Roman nobleman in a magnificent villa with a water supply. But the simple German had his own standard. A provincial legionnaire who has been marching for 30 days is a rough fellow. So a simple Germanic farmer might have looked much cleaner.

Thank you for your interest in part 1 of the interview with Lukas. We are happy to discuss the content here in the comments or on our Discord.

Best regards
Jens

notes.title: Weekly Blog 11
notes.content:
Hi everyone!

Felix here with another episode of our weekly blog. We’re still hard at work on our behind closed door demo for gamescom. It’s still far from where I’d like it to be but we’re progressing very fast.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/bc4946649b2d3fd7e70aa2afdff1abc467d6de57.gif[/img]

Originally I wanted to speak about our conquest system but we’re still breaking the vision down in tiers so I’ll save it for next time. Instead I’ll talk about an integral part of any survival game: food!

This is one of the features that has to be in the game because it’s something that survival game players come to expect but that we don’t consider one of our unique selling points in terms of features. Meaning we’re going to look at the competition and steal all of their best ideas! 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/bfabdc1ec28d885cfbbd07d9ed3ff40331479c63.jpg[/img]

The three survival games that came first to mind in terms of food when we went about this feature were:
Valheim: You can’t starve or die of thirst. You have 3 stomach slots that you have to fill with different food and drink items and each of them gives you a different buff to your health and your stamina pools and regeneration speeds as well as an optional additional buff. More complex food with harder to get ingredients give better buffs.

Icarus: Exactly the same as Valheim except you can die of starvation or dehydration.

Enshrouded: Also very close to Valheim but the buffs are more attribute related and you have to eat different categories of food: meats, vegetables, drinks, etc.

So as you can see, there is plenty of copying going around already and with good reason. None of these games consider food to be one of their main design pillars so it makes sense to take a system that’s not complicated and that works well. We’re going to go for the Valheim version because - while more realistic - we don’t consider starvation and dehydration to be fun mechanics in a game and the food categories element of Enshrouded makes sense for their attributes based system but we don’t have these.

So now we have a food system and it’s time to fill it with content. As in all survival games you’ll start out with nothing so the first foods you’ll be eating will be fruits and vegetables you can harvest in nature and eat raw or charred on a campfire followed by the meat of various animals you will hunt. The fun aspect will be once you’ll be able to do more complex recipes as that’s where we’ll be able to add the most flavor.

I’m by far not the Roman expert of the team - Jens thinks about the Roman Empire much more than I do - but even I know Romans knew how to eat! And Legionnaires had a pretty varied diet for soldiers. I’m told we will for sure have Puls (some sort of porridge) and Garum (fermented fish sauce used as condiment) in the game which both sound… really tasty? While we’ll have to figure out how to have it present in Teutoburg forest, wine in various forms (acidic, watered down, etc.) will have to play a role as well. I won’t give too many examples here due to my ignorance but we’re working closely with a historian that will help us add the proper food in the game and I’m looking forward to that.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/ba100791e393e98558b447ca1fb116cb5e7e2b23.jpg[/img]

On the topic of food in the game, we’ve also been talking to amazing book editors about making an accompanying Roman cookbook for the game. I’d be interested in hearing your thoughts about that for some sort of digital deluxe edition.

I’m sorry for the shorter update this week but there is so much to do and so little time. I’m off to go mine some more pixels and make this gamescom demo shine!

Felix

notes.title: Weekly Blog 10
notes.content:
Salvete my friends,

Lost Legions has made a significant leap forward in the last sprint, especially in the past week, and I couldn't be happier about it. We've known for a long time that our project has great potential, as there are already many systems that function well individually. Now, for the first time, the team has integrated these components into a cohesive flow. Immediately, the feeling of experiencing a real game emerges, rather than just individual parts.
We are working on the demo for Gamescom, which also marks the alpha milestone. Felix has designed the concept for the demo, which aims to showcase all the important elements of the game within 15 minutes. We are adhering to this strict time limit because we will only have short meetings with our guests at the fair. To minimize risks during the presentation, the demo will only be demonstrated in single-player mode.

In broad strokes, here is what will happen:
The player emerges from a tent in a small Roman camp. A superior soldier gives the player a selection of tasks, suggesting they can either handle them personally or delegate to NPCs. Additionally, preparations are underway for an attack on a Germanic village, which will commence shortly and which the player must lead, so haste is necessary.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/eb4d2fe7cf8ab33c0a9c36400bda8808e35d013e.jpg[/img]

Then the player gets to work. Various NPCs need to be addressed at different stations, providing the player with additional information to fulfill the tasks. Resources need to be procured, weapons upgraded, missing soldiers rescued, provisions restocked, and defenses expanded. There is much to do and many decisions to make.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/6f6ef307f29353b3ffc32ce8648ec1464ec95550.jpg[/img]

Once the path to the enemy village is clear, the attack can begin. A bloody skirmish takes place in the village square. After defeating the final boss, the player pursues the fleeing villagers into the misty swamp. Their trail disappears, and it becomes eerily quiet... too quiet... Something terrible emerges from the fog. The demo ends with an exciting revelation, hopefully leaving the audience eager for more.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/1328cabdf0441d0491d021e97034fd1de6b10d28.jpg[/img]

Previously, our game consisted of a large empty game world where various features could be tested independently at isolated locations. Since last week, however, we have reached a stage where these systems have gained meaningful context and build upon each other to convey a narrative arc. The current state still includes placeholders in many areas for final graphics. Voiceovers, effects, and animations are often still missing. Tasks cannot yet be delegated to NPCs. Closing these gaps, resolving issues, and enhancing gameplay will be our focus for the next 3.5 sprints leading up to Gamescom.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/e52790e6c6896ef6c8928fe0d96af7990b70071f.png[/img]

To achieve this ambitious goal, we need good organization of our workforce. If you want to get insight into our process:
Many work from home or optionally on-site in the co-working space at the S4G School for Games. Lost Legions is hosted as a repository on Github.com. From there, all developers can synchronize the latest version of the game to their PCs, upload their own new data, and make it available to others. Other files and documents are shared via a cloud service or our own NAS. In the art department, we use various tools for different applications: Blender for modeling and animation, Substance Suite for texturing. Additionally, tools like Krita, Photoshop, Clip Studio Paint are used. A newcomer is Cascadeur, for refining animations. Much of the work, such as programming via Blueprints, as well as VFX or level design, is done directly in the game engine, specifically Unreal Engine 5.3 in our case.

I've mentioned sprints several times. This term comes from the Agile SCRUM project management method. I want to note that we follow a heavily adapted version ourselves. Genuine SCRUM is something we cannot (yet) afford. A sprint for us spans two weeks and represents a development phase culminating in a new version of the game. It is planned with the premise: "What will increase the value of the product the most?" and "What do we most urgently need to reach the next milestone?" The entire team commits to this shared goal. Then the sprint is conducted undisturbed (hopefully), evaluated at the end, before the next interval begins. The contents implemented in successive sprints serve to achieve a milestone. For a game production like Lost Legions, these milestones are broadly divided into "Concept," "Pre-production," "Alpha," "Beta," and "Master."

In April, we completed the pre-production phase and have since been working towards our alpha milestone in August. In our case, this is very ambitious because it coincides with Gamescom, where we will present our game in the business area. So our goal is not only to achieve an alpha version of the game but also to create an impressive demo that our guests can play themselves!

So how does a sprint proceed?

Sprint Review & Planning
-Daily Scrum meetings: "What did I do yesterday?", "What do I plan to do today?"
-1-3 playtests with publishers or investors
-2 internal team playtests
-3-4 task force meetings
-Approximately 2 external/freelance meetings

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/d6247a97ae9efd94d41076f484e64e5923620026.png[/img]

This is just an example of the recurring and expected events during a sprint. It's also clear that only those involved in a role attend a meeting. We also try to schedule meetings mostly at the beginning of the week and in the morning, so the rest of the time can be used for free work. As a small team, we also organize a lot among ourselves and on the fly. This still works well in our structure, although it means documentation sometimes gets neglected. But that's a problem for future Tarock. What could possibly go wrong?

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/28ac0ca5a6fead80f5c6c10c63741944e500f3fb.jpg[/img]

I can tell you, experiencing ideas come to life as the parts come together is exactly the feeling that makes me not want to trade my profession for anything else! Our approach to establish the structure of the game as early as possible, so we have something that can be further developed, is paying off in my opinion. I look forward to detailing the demo in the coming weeks and am eager to see the reactions in Cologne.
As a closing remark, I would like to send a big thank you to the entire team who have made phenomenal efforts to reach this state!

Best regards,
Jens

notes.title: Weekly Blog 9
notes.content:
Hi everyone!

Felix here with another episode of our weekly blog. We’ve been hard at work the past few weeks. Gamescom is coming up, and we’re building a near-final quality demo to show to the press behind closed doors during the event. It’s a lot of stress but also exhilarating to see the game progress so fast.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/a1b1f0c538959c30705eb8b56b7d5221726b813b.jpg[/img]

I’ve been working on transferring the feature I consider my baby from the pre-production prototype to our development build: NPC Management! The idea for this feature came when I played the excellent Medieval Dynasty and was slightly disappointed when my villagers didn’t actually go into the woods to cut wood or hunt and instead made the resources magically appear in the stockpile. Then came the Bellwright steam fest demo (didn’t find the time yet to try the full game) and the villagers would actually go cut down the trees and transport the wood, but I felt restricted by having to assign them specific jobs. Wouldn’t it be fun to have a similar job system as in Colony Sim games like Rimworld, Dwarf Fortress, or even Prison Architect, where the player creates jobs in the world, assigns some priorities to them and some preferences for the villagers, and then have the idle villagers pick their own job?

Well, this is basically the vision of what the management will be in Lost Legions. Currently, we’re at what I’d call Tier 1 of this feature. NPC legionaries will roam about their assigned camp and idle about when there is nothing to do. The player can run around the world and designate things that they want transported back to the camp, trees they want to have cut down, or even plan out structures they want to have built or items they want to have crafted. Each of these orders will add a job to a queue in the camp, and the next free legionary will take on the job and attempt to complete it. Once they are done with one job, they will look for the next and go back to idling if there is nothing to do.

The main benefit here is that players can delegate the grind to NPCs while still being very much in control of what will actually be done (down to which tree exactly is to be cut and which one is not, for example) while at the same time not having to move the NPCs around different jobs if there are fewer of them than kinds of things to be done. Additionally, the planning feature enables you to design where buildings will have to be and what items you want to craft before actually having the resources. If you then also give your soldiers the order to gather the required resources while you are out exploring, everything will be crafted and built once you come back as the planned build order becomes active once the resources are there.

Now as for why this is Tier 1: currently, there is absolutely no UI where you can see what orders are active, what order they are in, and what an NPC is actually doing. Everything happens under the hood, but there still needs to be a lot of communication. I’m thinking task lists like Dwarf Fortress and priority lists like Rimworld at the moment.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/d0a3422c38038bcf1967665422973f506e66d82e.png[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/34d392922f5427dbee2fe981aa91a677d859d9a0.png[/img]

Another problem is that you have to make each job individually. It’s fine for planning out a build order or a craft order, but selecting each tree that has to be cut down individually doesn’t feel fun after a while. There I want to work on order posts you can place in the forest that will define a radius of trees to be cut down… I need to test this out to see how it feels.

Something that already works and is pretty awesome is that you can run up to any soldier and draft him. Similar to drafting in Rimworld, the NPC will drop everything, put its current order back in the list, and start following you around and fighting with you. Very Tier 0 still, as currently you can’t equip them with weapons and armor, but the potential is there!

I hope I could give you some insight into this feature that I’m very excited about. There’s a lot of work being done on other great parts of the game at the moment, and I think we’ll have nice new things to show you all at Gamescom.

For now though: back to the pixel mines!

Felix

Salvete amici mei,
In the best sense of a developer diary, today I'm sharing with you what has occupied us over the past week.

The biggest change in our mode is certainly the start of the internship period.

Back in early March, I introduced our studio and the project to the students for the first time at the S4G Recruitment Day. Since then, an application process took place, resulting in eight (8!) interns.

Last week, we finally moved into a room at the S4G School for Games as a co-working space, where the core team also has the opportunity to leave the confines of their home offices and return to staring at monitors and loading bars in real human company.

We’ve been working together for a week now, and I couldn’t be happier with our new circumstances. Everyone is super committed, fully immersed in the project both mentally and practically, and has high standards for themselves and our game.

Thanks to this support, we are able to tackle some topics that we otherwise wouldn’t have been able to address in the alpha phase.

[b]Character & Environment Concept Art [/b]
- We are using Unreal’s Metahumans. Despite all the advantages, it quickly becomes clear: the base characters are very generic. Thanks to the developed backstories for each character, our concept artist can create designs to make the characters look more interesting. 

- The most important character in Lost Legions is certainly the environment. To give the locations in the game the right atmosphere, another artist is designing distinctive interaction points and landmarks. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/eff5a2e115f766bd3be5954dc670e5e2ea779247.png[/img]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/dcbc3faa69508214d253e0f9f0b266cc0ed7c9fb.png[/img]

[b]UX Flow and UI Design [/b]
To develop quickly and efficiently, our game is based on a combination of pre-made frameworks. We omit certain functions, expand others, or add new ones. To turn this mosaic back into a cohesive and easily understandable whole, the user interface must be well planned and designed. For this important task, we were able to secure a dedicated designer. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/20ce1a74f91d06ad0bfcdb8e69a14c649fd17edd.png[/img]

[b]Level and Quest Design [/b]
Under Uschi’s leadership, two other interns are working on the actual implementation of the game content. What is there to discover? What is my goal? Who stands in my way and what is the reward for my effort? In this exciting area, all fields of work come together. Scenography, lighting, camera, sound, and acting down to the fog machine, everything has to be considered.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/51c6382705f571068f2a7de2ce818f85eaef07db.png[/img]

[b]Combat Effects (Blood & Gore!!) [/b]
An important aspect of the game that we want to improve by the alpha milestone in August is combat. A function we have lacked so far, but from which we hope for a big impact, is visual effects as feedback for player inputs. To put it simply: blood should splatter, sparks should fly. 
Players should clearly see whether they hit or get hit. An experienced programmer, who uses the S4G training program to specialize in this area, is creating something splashy for us. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/39e4b8d997a2d480bc1d1c177cf838a47276e901.gif[/img]

[b]Behavior of Animals and NPCs [/b]
Another trainee programmer is supporting Felix and Stephan from the core team to bring better NPC behaviors into the game. Our first project is to see if we can make Unreal’s standard wolf and deer more believable and, from a player’s perspective, give them more interesting behavior. 

[b]Improvement of Animations [/b]
Together with a talented 3D and tech artist, I am setting up a pipeline to improve or replace the currently used animations. We are looking for solutions to add more bones to the Metahuman skeleton to handle certain special cases. Right now, we are even experimenting with AI-supported solutions like Cascadeur. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/a0c8ac84025907edc875573d52f19cdcee946732.png[/img]

[b]More Items, Clothing [/b]
Incidentally, he is also creating more objects to fill in some content gaps, so that the demo at Gamescom appears as comprehensive as possible. For example, he implemented a clever system to apply fur, based on a modern programmatic solution using Blender’s Geometry Nodes. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/26fd69514c4e6f9b5b2214a2c2ce080b631fa2fc.gif[/img]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/fa2b3f34a4ccf26120eded6b421a13b1cb7c70de.gif[/img]

As hoped and (to be honest) also planned, the handpicked students are doing excellent work. 
This is of course a testament to each and every one of them, who bring their creativity and work ethic to our service. But I also want to point out that the training at S4G School for Games proves to me every year that it trains directly for the industry. 
The graduates are so familiar with the usual workflows of the games industry that they can jump right in without lengthy onboarding. As a studio, we get additional manpower, which we are very grateful for right before Gamescom. The trainees get the opportunity to contribute to a commercial game development as part of their training and will be credited at the end. 

I am looking forward to the time together and the great new content in the game that we will create together.

Best regards, 

Jens

notes.title: Weekly Blog 7
notes.content:
Hi everyone!

Felix here with the weekly blog. Over the last couple of weeks, we’ve delved into our game design pillars and how we define and develop features. Today, I want to tackle another crucial subject that influences the entire design of our game: USPs – or unique selling points. Let's explore how these USPs translate into the game's design.
Before diving in, I have some exciting news! Today, we welcomed 8 interns to help us with the game and the press demo for Gamescom. My cofounder Jens has been leading the game art teaching department at the School 4 Games in Berlin for many years. This partnership allows us to work with his best and brightest students during their obligatory internships each year. It’s a win-win: they get hands-on experience working on an actual game with a mentor they already know, and we get a significant development boost.
As part of their introduction today, we had a passion transfer meeting where we showed them all the driving forces behind the game, including the USPs and how we integrate them into the game. Now, I'm excited to pass this on to you, fresh from our meeting!

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/68815cfc124ae6210d4720f55e2328c92d965e56.jpg[/img]
(That’s me, the bearded guy with the Star Wars shirt on the bottom right.)

So, in order in which we presented the today, our unique selling points are:

[b]Historical[/b]

One of our core USPs is historical accuracy. This should be pretty obvious, but it’s important to mention that we strive to incorporate this element into all our games. That's why we collaborate closely with Humboldt University to ensure we remain as accurate as possible.
So, what does this mean for Lost Legions specifically? It means the game's premise is based on historical events – the Battle of Teutoburger Forest actually happened. We meticulously represent every piece of equipment, especially the well-documented kits of Roman Legionaries. Additionally, we use noninvasive means to convey historical knowledge, similar to item descriptions in Dark Souls games, but grounded in real history.
Now, some of you might have noticed mystical elements in the trailer and wondered how they fit into our historically accurate world. Without spoiling too much, I can assure you that any mystical elements are rooted in the mythology and beliefs of the time. In that era, gods and spirits were believed to be very active. However, there was a clear distinction between the feats of gods, spirits, and monsters and the capabilities of mortals, even the best Legionaries. So, no worries about fireball-throwing centurions in our game!

[b]Optional[/b]

This USP is a bit less straightforward but ties in beautifully with our game design pillars. Survival games cater to a diverse range of player types. Whether you love exploring, building a practical fort, or fighting the biggest creatures, there's something for everyone. But what about the tasks you don't enjoy?
Personally, I love exploring but find building bases and collecting resources tedious. I play with a friend who will build a city overnight but isn't keen on combat. It's great when playing with friends who have diverse interests, but what if you're not?
Enter the idea of optionality. Our vision is to allow players to delegate major game tasks to NPC Legionaries. They can gather resources, craft items, build structures, and even explore or fight on your behalf. Examples of how this concept permeates the game can be found everywhere: We're also exploring the idea of including minigames for crafting. So according with the principle, these should be optional and not penalize players who choose not to engage with them.
I'm excited to see how far we can take this concept, but it’s already proving valuable in our design process.

[b]Narrative[/b]

Last, but definitely not least, is the narrative. We want to tell an epic story that you can enjoy alone or with friends. This means borrowing a bit from role-playing games to set the scene and tell engaging stories. It creates challenges, especially with the "with friends" component, but it’s one of the aspects I'm most excited about. I love deep, engaging stories in games, and I can’t wait to create one for you. 😊
With that said, I hear the pixel mines calling…

See you next time!

Felix

notes.title: Weekly Blog 5
notes.content:
Hey everyone,

It's Felix again! I wanted to dive deeper into one of our game pillars today, but I kept struggling with how to best describe it. Our approach to game design and development might be familiar to those in the games industry since it’s based on conventional agile software development methods. However, it can be a bit complicated to describe future features because it’s not always clear how much of the original concept will be implemented.

We’re calling our version of agile development the tiered approach, and I think this image that stuck with me from back in my uni days describes it best:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/8834773cee03913cea1fe5115d0e5e0f58a8a260.png[/img]


Basically, when we design a feature for the game, we first write down what the best possible version of the feature would be if we had infinite resources and time (The sports car in the example). 
We call this Tier 4 or 5, depending on the complexity of the feature. From there, we go back to Tier 1 and imagine the most basic version of the feature that does the same in spirit but without any bells and whistles, and is the fastest to implement (The skateboard is also a wheeled vehicle that takes you faster from A to B). Tiers 2 and 3 are then used to fill the gap by spreading the development amount as evenly as possible. All tiers must enable their game mechanic in the game, just with increasing complexity and, hopefully, fun. (Some people find motorbikes more fun than cars if we stick with the analogy.)

When we develop, we go through all features and implement the first tier. We’re more or less at this stage now. The big advantage is that we can get a clear picture of the game and what it will be at the end very early, and we get to play and test it internally very fast. Actually, we’ve been playing the game weekly since the first month of development—something I’ve never been able to do before.

From there, we’ll develop higher and higher tiers for each feature, focusing on improving the tiers of core features and those that suffer the most in terms of fun at lower tiers.

This approach gives us many advantages. We’ll have a playable game out to you much faster, we can make adjustments along the way more easily, and overall the development is much safer, meaning there will be a game at the end of all this for sure.

Of course, there are always drawbacks: this approach probably requires more effort overall as we will end up reworking features repeatedly. This is more of a non-drawback, however, since the reworks will be in favor of better overall quality. 
The second big drawback is that it makes it very difficult to talk about features early. Should we talk about Tier 5 with the risk of changing it completely until we get there or—worst case scenario—only getting to Tier 3 during development? Or should we play it safe and talk about lower tiers with the risk of sounding more generic?

Now that I’ve explained our process, I feel more confident about taking a third approach: transparently discussing the tiers of the features we’re currently considering with the knowledge that we’re mostly at Tier 1 and that a lot of things might change on the way to Tier 5. ^^

I’m looking forward to telling you more about features with this in mind. As always, I’m excited to hear your thoughts! For now, though, it's back to the pixel mines for me. See you next week!

Cheers, Felix

notes.title: Weekly Blog 4
notes.content:
Salvete amici mei,
The (urgently needed) holiday on Monday and my class today have almost thrown us off our weekly Dev-Blog routine. Don't worry! I have things to tell you and I want to get them off of my chest now: This week I want to talk about how we deal with "history" and maybe give you a little taste of what we can expect from Lost Legions.

First of all, let me emphasize that our mission at Tarock Interactive is to develop games based on actual historical events or episodes. This means that we want to immerse our players in game worlds where history comes alive. We believe that there are fresh perspectives that we want to implement in games. Our titles should put you in the shoes of ordinary people who have to experience a historical timeline, unable to change the course of events, but still having the task of dealing with the circumstances to try to make the best of it or simply stay alive.

Lost Legions is Tarock's first game, but it is by no means the first one developed by our team. However, since we have just started with the new studio, Lost Legions takes a special position in many ways.
Regarding this week's topic: Lost Legions will not be our most historically accurate game, as we will take many creative liberties to bring the "exaggerated" game world to life and tell the adventure we have come up with. On the other hand, the factual basis and starting point of the game as well as its presentation should be as historically correct as possible.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/8496242771aa05a99db8c42fc6ce2ca09e307212.png[/img]

I'm trying not to reveal anything about the game's mysterious story, but I want you to feel confident that the "creative liberties" are supported by established literature. I'm telling you this because I feel that it's time to manage some expectations about our game. From the way the game is being discussed online, I understand that some people want to see a super realistic "life simulator about the Roman army". Although I also find this concept very fascinating, Lost Legions was never intended to be such a game.

By the way the entire team is working on this game, I am absolutely convinced that we will stay true to the theme and deliver a worthy adventure in ancient Rome that satisfies both fans of the gameplay genre and history enthusiasts. We simply have to achieve that, because our commitment to this production should lead to a successful release of the game and enable us to grow our company to a size where we can afford to have full-time historical advisors on the team. (No Pressure, Go Team!)
This, in turn, ensures that future games are created with the active support and consultation of professional historians. This allows us to recreate and simulate history like never before using modern real-time technology. The foundation for this collaboration has already been laid through close cooperation with the Humboldt University of Berlin, where our research is supported by the Department of Ancient Archaeology.

I hope this sheds some light on our approach to developing historical games.
Feel free to continue the discussion here and on our Discord. I look forward to hearing your thoughts.

Best regards,
Jens

notes.title: Weekly Blog 3
notes.content:
Hey everyone,

It's Felix again! Today, I’m excited to sketch out the main gameplay pillars of Lost Legions for you. This is just a broad overview to give you a taste of what’s to come, and I’ll dive deeper into each aspect in future posts.

I’m a huge fan of survival crafting games, and with Lost Legions, we’ve aimed to blend the best features of some of my favorites, infuse our unique twists, and strip away any annoying bits.

[b]Our game is built around three main interconnected pillars: Exploration, Management, and Conquest.[/b]

[b]Management[/b]: Drawing inspiration from games like Medieval Dynasty and Bellwright, we’ve designed a system where you can delegate the grindy tasks to NPCs. Whether you’re adventuring or battling, your NPCs will be busy gathering resources, crafting items, and shuttling supplies between camps. You’ll need to strategically manage your limited manpower, especially since resources are often location-specific and your NPCs are at risk of capture by Germanic forces. For the big Roman engineering feats in the game, you’ll be tasked with collecting massive resource hauls from various regions to a central project site.

[b]Exploration[/b]: Balancing freedom and storytelling in an open world survival game is tricky. Subnautica did an incredible job at this, and we’re taking a page from their book. While you’re free to explore, you’ll be able to use NPCs to subtly guide you. Scouts can be sent out to identify and report back on unexplored points of interest, giving you hints and directions only when you want them, ensuring you have total control over your exploration experience.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/9279374221f11e23e518d5543c83f56c852f4fd6.png[/img]

[b]Conquest[/b]: Last but certainly not least, we have conquest. Stranded behind enemy lines in hostile territory, feeling constantly under threat is crucial. We’re taking inspiration from games like 7 Days to Die and Conan Exiles and their periodic raids and adding to it. Players will defend and also have opportunities to conquer predetermined enemy bases and villages. The locations for building most structures are limited to these base locations, adding a layer of strategic planning as each location has its unique advantages, like access to specific resources or key tactical positions. You’ll need to fortify these bases with walls, traps, and other defenses to repel the barbarians while also gearing up for your counterattacks. Every captured base could be regained by the enemy, making for a dynamic tug of war.

I hope this gives you a better sense of what to expect from the game. There’s a lot more to unpack about each pillar, and I’ll get into those details in upcoming posts. I’m also eager to discuss some quality of life features that we’re really excited about.

Looking forward to hearing your thoughts on this! For now, it's back to the pixel mines for me. See you next week!

Cheers, Felix

notes.content:

Our announcement last week really blew us away with your reactions and support—thank you! It’s made us eager to open up more about what we’re doing and why. [img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/b0017c1a32b6aaa7057a3b3f9ca53742eb65da3a.jpg[/img]

Today, I want to touch on a few things you’ve brought up since our big reveal:

[b]Quality of Animations and Effects:[/b] A lot of you pointed out concerns here. Just to clear things up, the footage we showed is from a pre-alpha stage. We’re on it, aiming for major improvements as we head towards launch. Plus, the positive buzz has opened up new doors for funding which means we can hopefully beef up our resources in this department.

[b]Our Team:[/b] There’s six of us, with five of us hacking away down in the pixel mines of development. Each of us has been in the game industry for an average of 12 years, so we know our stuff. We’re small, but that gives us agility and lets us take some creative leaps—don’t expect AAA scope, but do expect some surprises.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/e9307d2e864c3f5f787022f90890fe790f80b8f4.jpg[/img]

[b]Narrative Focus:[/b] Lost Legions isn’t just another open world survival crafting game. We’re weaving a strong narrative thread that sets our game apart. This focus on storytelling is why we’re capping multiplayer sessions at four players—it keeps the story tight and engaging for everyone.

[b]Game Design Pillars:[/b] Mechanically, Lost Legions is designed around three core pillars: exploration, conquest, and management. We’re excited to tell you more about what that means and how we’re giving each of those pillars a Roman twist.

[b]Big in Japan:[/b] Wow, we did not see that coming! We’re thrilled by the interest from Japan and promise a professional localization. We want everyone to feel right at home in the game.
Thanks for making this such an exciting time for us. We can’t wait to dive deeper into these topics and more in our upcoming posts.

Catch you next week,
Felix

notes.title: In new open world game Lost Legions you are a Roman "rebuilding the empire" behind enemy lines
notes.content:
The announcement trailer for Lost Legions opens with a Roman Emperor bellowing “GIVE ME BACK MY LEGIONS” like a kid who’s just had his pudding taken away. I'd just had a big swig of coffee before watching, and was instantly swept off by visions of an apoplectic Roman bigwig rampaging through the forests of darkest Germania, gluing abducted legionnaires together into a sort of Octavian katamari... and then they revealed that it’s another open world survival game, with no less than two trailer beats dedicated to the act of hacking down a tree.

I mean no disrespect to developers Tarock Interactive - they're not to blame for my addled imagination - but there are many open world survival games and as a weary Ed Thorn recently noted, the majority are heavily frontloaded with wilderness carpentry. I don’t think survival games should emphasise wood-chopping in their announcement footage. It's like doing a Call of Duty montage of people getting shot three seconds from spawn. Still, if there's no katamari mechanic, the idea of raising a small army of mostly AI-controlled Roman soldiers behind enemy lines has a certain charm. Without further ado, here’s the trailer.
